pericopes.text: For behold, it came to pass that fifty and five years had passed away, from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem; wherefore, Nephi gave me, Jacob, a commandment concerning the small plates, upon which these things are engraven.

And he gave me, Jacob, a commandment that I should write upon these plates, a few of the things which I considered to be most precious: that I should not touch, save it were lightly, concerning the history of this people which are called the people of Nephi.
For he said that the history of his people should be engraven upon his other plates, and that I should preserve these plates, and hand them down unto my seed, from generation to generation.

And if there were preaching which was sacred, or revelation which was great, or prophesying, that I should engraven the heads of them upon these plates, and touch upon them as much as it were possible, for Christ’s sake, and for the sake of our people:

provenance.other: “for Christ's sake” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (1 Corinthians 4:10, 2 Corinthians 12:10, Ephesians 4:32), and in none of them is the phrase continued. Only Romans 15:30 runs on as Jacob does — 'for the Lord Jesus Christ's sake, and for the love of the Spirit' — giving the five-word sequence 'Christ's sake, and for the' that Jacob completes with 'sake of our people'.
provenance.significance: Romans 15:30 is Paul asking a church to strive together with him in prayer; Jacob 1:4 is Jacob explaining what will be allowed onto a plate too small to hold a history. Both sentences name two beneficiaries of an effort, Christ first and a people second, in the same double construction. What the borrowing does to the colophon is make the criterion of selection apostolic rather than archival: the plates keep preaching, revelation and prophecy 'for Christ's sake, and for the sake of our people' because that is the pair Paul's request already assumes.

links.note: 'That I should engraven the heads of them upon these plates, and touch upon them as much as it were possible, for Christ's sake, and for the sake of our people.' The phrase 'for Christ's sake' occurs in exactly three KJV verses and stands alone in all of them; the doubled form Jacob uses, with 'and for the' following, is Romans 15:30's alone. This falls far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation and is catalogued as an allusion accordingly — the evidence is the shape of the sequence, not its length.
links.text: Now I beseech you, brethren, for the Lord Jesus Christ’s sake, and for the love of the Spirit, that ye strive together with me in your prayers to God for me;

pericopes.text: for because of faith and great anxiety, it truly had been made manifest unto us concerning our people, what things should happen unto them.

provenance.other: “what things should happen” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 10:32, where the object is 'unto him'. Jacob 1:5 has the same four words with 'unto them'. The parallel at Mark 10:32 in the other Synoptics does not use the construction.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing supplies the chapter's whole argument. Mark 10:32 is the third passion prediction: Jesus takes the twelve apart on the road to Jerusalem to tell them 'what things should happen unto him', and the next verses are the betrayal, the mocking, the scourging and the killing. Jacob 1:5 has that clause for a revelation about his own people; 1:6 immediately says 'we knew of Christ and his Kingdom, which should come'; and 1:8 asks all men to 'view his death, and suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world'. The one KJV verse behind Jacob's foreknowledge is Christ's foreknowledge of his own passion, and the three verses that follow it in Jacob are about exactly that.

links.note: 'It truly had been made manifest unto us concerning our people, what things should happen unto them.' A four-word KJV singleton, and the sense transfers cleanly: a private disclosure to a small group of what is coming. The link is proposed on rarity plus the sequence that follows it — Jacob moves from the disclosure (1:5) to knowing Christ (1:6) to viewing his death (1:8), which is the order of Mark 10:32-34.
links.text: And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem; and Jesus went before them: and they were amazed; and as they followed, they were afraid. And he took again the twelve, and began to tell them what things should happen unto him,

pericopes.text: And we also had many revelations, and the spirit of much prophecy; wherefore, we knew of Christ and his Kingdom, which should come.

provenance.other: “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10 — 'the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy'. Jacob 1:6 reads 'the spirit of much prophecy', which is the singleton with one word inserted.
provenance.significance: Revelation 19:10's clause is a definition, not a description: it identifies the spirit of prophecy with the testimony of Jesus. Jacob 1:6 says 'we also had many revelations, and the spirit of much prophecy; wherefore, we knew of Christ and his Kingdom, which should come' — and the 'wherefore' does what Revelation's copula does, deriving the knowledge of Christ from the spirit of prophecy. Neither verse argues the point; Revelation states it and Jacob infers from it.

links.note: 'And we also had many revelations, and the spirit of much prophecy.' The phrase is a KJV singleton, and Jacob's insertion of 'much' is the kind of adaptation the 1830 text makes freely. Catalogued as an echo rather than an allusion because four words with an interpolation is thin contact and the phrase had long since entered ordinary religious English; what recommends it is that Jacob's next clause performs the equation Revelation 19:10 makes.
links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, we laboured diligently among our people, that we might persuade them to come unto Christ, and partake of the goodness of God, that they might enter into his rest, lest by any means he should swear in his wrath they should not enter in, as in the provocation in the days of temptation, while the children of Israel were in the wilderness.—

provenance.mt: Psalm 95:8 — 'Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, AND AS IN the day of temptation in the wilderness'; Psalm 95:11 — 'Unto whom I sware in MY wrath that they should not enter into MY rest.'
provenance.route: Psalm 95:8-11 via Hebrews 3:8-18 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The mediation is decided twice over, at two places where the KJV's psalm and the KJV's epistle differ. (1) “enter into his rest” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 3:18 — 'And to whom sware he that they should not enter into his rest' — which is the epistle's third-person recasting of the psalm's first-person 'into my rest'. “into my rest” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (Psalm 95:11, Hebrews 3:11, Hebrews 4:3, Hebrews 4:5). Jacob 1:7 has 'enter into his rest' and 'he should swear in his wrath', both third person, against the psalm's 'I sware in my wrath … my rest'. (2) Psalm 95:8 reads 'as in the provocation, AND AS IN the day of temptation'; Hebrews 3:8 drops 'and as' and reads 'as in the provocation, in the day of temptation'. Jacob reads 'as in the provocation in the days of temptation' — continuous, without the psalm's second 'as in'. “as in the provocation” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, Psalm 95:8, Hebrews 3:8 and Hebrews 3:15, all of one text and its epistle. tools/mediation-check.py returns 'no decisive divergence' on both pairs, because its word alignment cannot register an ABSENCE (Hebrews' distinctive reading at 3:8 is the omission of 'and as') and because it compares only the two candidates named to it; the singleton count at 'enter into his rest' is what settles the case, and it settles it for Hebrews.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's spine and the pilot's kind of finding: a passage everyone reads as Psalm 95 turns out, at every point where the two testaments part, to have the epistle's wording. And the epistle's wording is not neutral. Psalm 95:11 is God's oath about a generation already dead; Hebrews 3-4 turns it into a live threat to its own readers, argues that the rest was never entered and remains open, and grounds the exhortation in 3:1's 'partakers of the heavenly calling' and 3:14's 'partakers of Christ'. Jacob 1:7 has that too — 'partake of the goodness of God' — and its purpose clause, persuading a people to come to Christ so that they may enter the rest they might otherwise be sworn out of, is Hebrews' argument in one sentence rather than the psalm's. The 'lest by any means' that governs the threat is likewise Pauline: it occurs in exactly three KJV verses, 1 Corinthians 8:9, 2 Corinthians 11:3 and Galatians 2:2.
provenance.alternative: Psalm 95:8-11 is the ultimate source and Hardy's apparatus names it first; the claim here is only about which English wording is being followed, not about which text is being remembered.

links.note: 'That they might enter into his rest, lest by any means he should swear in his wrath they should not enter in, as in the provocation in the days of temptation, while the children of Israel were in the wilderness.' Hardy's cross-references at this verse are Psalm 95:8, Hebrews 3:8, Psalm 95:8-11 and, for the underlying episodes, Exodus 17:1-7 and Numbers 20:2-13 — the waters of Massah and Meribah, which Exodus 17:7 names for the chiding and the tempting. What this catalogue adds is the mediation. Jacob has the New Testament form at both points of divergence: 'enter into his rest' rather than 'into my rest', which occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that verse is Hebrews 3:18; and 'as in the provocation in the days of temptation' run continuously, without the 'and as' that Psalm 95:8 interposes and Hebrews 3:8 removes. The 1830 'days' for Hebrews' 'day' is Jacob's own, and 1920 did not correct it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 1.7 (Psalm 95:8; Hebrews 3:8; Psalm 95:8-11; Exodus 17:1-7; Numbers 20:2-13)
links.text: Harden not your hearts, as in the provocation, in the day of temptation in the wilderness:

provenance.other: “the children of Israel were in the wilderness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Numbers 15:32. Jacob 1:7 closes with the whole of it, conjunction included: 'while the children of Israel were in the wilderness'. Hebrews 3:8, which supplies the rest of the sentence, ends at 'in the wilderness' and does not name Israel.
provenance.significance: The clause is a gloss: Hebrews 3:8 says only 'in the wilderness', and Jacob adds the subject from the one KJV verse that has it. What that verse then contains is a wilderness provocation of its own — the man found gathering sticks on the sabbath, brought to Moses, and stoned by the whole congregation at the Lord's word (Numbers 15:32-36). So a sentence warning a people not to be sworn out of God's rest ends by quoting the setting of the KJV's sharpest wilderness punishment, and the eight words that fill out Hebrews' geography carry a story of a congregation executing one of its own for refusing rest on the day appointed for it.

links.note: 'As in the provocation in the days of temptation, while the children of Israel were in the wilderness.' An eight-word KJV singleton, and its position is exactly where Hebrews 3:8 stops. Confidence is moderate rather than high because the string is a natural way to say an ordinary thing and the writer had every reason to name Israel here whether or not Numbers 15:32 was in view; the case rests on the fact that the KJV says it in this order in one place only, and on the subject matter of that place.
links.text: And while the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man that gathered sticks upon the sabbath day.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, we would to God that we could persuade all men not to rebel against God, to provoke him to anger, but that all men would believe in Christ, and view his death, and suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world; wherefore, I, Jacob, take it upon me to fulfil the commandment of my brother Nephi.

provenance.other: “would to God” occurs in exactly six KJV verses (Exodus 16:3, Joshua 7:7, Judges 9:29, Acts 26:29, 1 Corinthians 4:8, 2 Corinthians 11:1). In five of them the wish is a complaint or a piece of sarcasm — that Israel had died in Egypt, that they had dwelt beyond Jordan, that Paul's readers really did reign. Acts 26:29 is the only KJV verse in which the wish is that other people were Christians, and it is spoken in immediate answer to a sentence about persuasion.
provenance.significance: Agrippa says 'Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian', and Paul answers 'I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.' Jacob 1:8 puts the two halves back together: 'we would to God that we could persuade all men … that all men would believe in Christ.' The persuasion Agrippa declines and the wish Paul makes over him are one sentence in Jacob, and what Paul wishes them into — 'such as I am, except these bonds' — Jacob spells out as viewing his death, suffering his cross, and bearing the shame of the world. Paul's exception for his chains is precisely what Jacob refuses to except.

links.note: 'Wherefore, we would to God that we could persuade all men not to rebel against God … but that all men would believe in Christ.' The wish and the persuading belong together in exactly one KJV place, Acts 26:28-29, and Jacob has both, in Paul's order and with Paul's universal extension ('all that hear me this day' / 'all men'). Confidence is held at moderate because 'would to God' occurs in exactly six KJV verses and had long been ordinary English; the argument is the collocation with persuasion and belief in Christ, not the idiom.
links.text: And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.

provenance.route: Hebrews 12:2 (the pairing) + Ezekiel 34:29 (the wording of 'bear the shame') → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “endured the cross” and “despising the shame” each occur in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Hebrews 12:2: the cross and the shame are joined nowhere else in the KJV. The wording of Jacob's second clause is Ezekiel's, however — “bear the shame” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 34:29 ('neither bear the shame of the heathen any more'), which supplies the whole five-word run 'bear the shame of the'.
provenance.significance: Jacob has run the two through each other and reversed both. Hebrews 12:2 has Christ enduring the cross and DESPISING the shame; Jacob asks the reader to 'suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world' — the same pair, transferred from Christ to the disciple, with despising turned into bearing. Ezekiel 34:29 is a promise that a restored people will never again bear the shame of the heathen; Jacob asks his people to take up the shame of the world voluntarily. The borrowing is doing theological work in both directions: what Christ despised the disciple carries, and what the shepherd-oracle promised to lift off Israel is picked back up on purpose.
provenance.alternative: Matthew 16:24's 'take up his cross, and follow me' is the more familiar source for a cross laid on the disciple, and 'suffer his cross' may be no more than that; what Matthew has not got is the shame.

links.note: 'That all men would believe in Christ, and view his death, and suffer his cross, and bear the shame of the world.' The KJV joins a cross to a shame in exactly one verse, Hebrews 12:2, and Jacob has the pair in Hebrews' order while taking the words 'bear the shame of the' from the only KJV verse that contains them, Ezekiel 34:29. Moderate rather than high: neither source is reproduced as a clause, and the composite reading is this catalogue's proposal.
links.text: Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.

pericopes.text: Now Nephi began to be old, and he saw that he must soon die; wherefore, he anointed a man to be a king and a ruler over his people now, according to the reigns of the kings.—

provenance.other: “man to be a ruler over” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 6:5: 'neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel'. Jacob 1:9 reads 'he anointed a man to be a king and a ruler over his people' — the singleton with two words inserted and the pronoun turned from 'my' to 'his'. “ruler over his people” occurs in no KJV verse at all; “ruler over my people” occurs in exactly four (2 Samuel 7:8, 1 Chronicles 11:2, 1 Chronicles 17:7, 2 Chronicles 6:5), and all four are about David.
provenance.significance: The one KJV sentence about appointing a man to be a ruler over the people is spoken by Solomon, at the dedication of the temple, and its content is a refusal: God chose no city and no man until he chose David and Jerusalem. Jacob 1:9 uses it for the moment the Nephites acquire a monarchy; Jacob 1:15 records what the monarchy immediately produced, 'such as like unto David of Old, desiring many wives and concubines, and also Solomon, his son'; and Jacob 1:17 has Jacob preaching against it in the temple. The chapter borrows the words of Solomon's temple prayer to install a king, and eight verses later is standing in a temple denouncing the people for imitating Solomon.

links.note: 'Wherefore, he anointed a man to be a king and a ruler over his people now, according to the reigns of the kings.' The phrase 'man to be a ruler over' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and the two words Jacob inserts into it ('a king and') are the point of the sentence — 2 Chronicles 6:5 concerns choosing a ruler, and Jacob's people are getting a king. The anointing itself is the Samuel formula (1 Samuel 9:16, 'thou shalt anoint him to be captain over my people'), for which Jacob substitutes the Chronicler's noun.
links.text: Since the day that I brought forth my people out of the land of Egypt I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build an house in, that my name might be there; neither chose I any man to be a ruler over my people Israel:

pericopes.text: The people having loved Nephi exceedingly, he having been a great protector for them, having wielded the sword of Laban in their defence, and having laboured in all his days for their welfare;

wherefore, the people were desirous to retain in remembrance his name. And whoso should reign in his stead, were called by the people Second Nephi, Third Nephi, &c. according to the reigns of the kings; and thus they were called by the people, let them be of whatever name they would.
And it came to pass that Nephi died.
Now the people which were not Lamanites, were Nephites; nevertheless, they were called Nephites, Jacobites, Josephites, Zoramites, Lamanites, Lemuelites, and Ishmaelites.

But I, Jacob, shall not hereafter distinguish them by these names, but I shall call them Lamanites. They that seek to destroy the people of Nephi, and they which are friendly to Nephi, I shall call Nephites, or the people of Nephi, according to the reigns of the kings.

And now it came to pass that the people of Nephi, under the reign of the second king, began to grow hard in their hearts, and indulge themselves somewhat in wicked practices, such as like unto David of Old, desiring many wives and concubines, and also Solomon, his son;

provenance.mt: 1 Kings 11:3 — 'And he had seven hundred wives, princesses, and three hundred concubines: and his wives turned away his heart.'
provenance.route: 2 Samuel 5:13 + 1 Kings 11:1-3, against Deuteronomy 17:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “concubines and wives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:13, and it is about David; Jacob 1:15 has the pair in the reverse order, 'many wives and concubines', which is no KJV string. The KJV never brings David's concubines and Solomon's wives into one sentence — 2 Samuel 5:13 and 1 Kings 11:1-3 are five centuries and eight books apart — and Jacob's pairing of the two is an act of reading, not of quotation.
provenance.significance: The law behind the complaint is Deuteronomy 17:17, the law of the king: 'Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.' 1 Kings 11:3 reports the exact failure the law names — 'his wives turned away his heart' — and Jacob 1:15 reports it in a third nation, one verse after 'the second king' takes the throne and in the same breath as 'began to grow hard in their hearts'. The Nephite monarchy is being judged by the Deuteronomic law of the king within a verse of its founding, and Jacob 2 will make that judgment explicit.

links.note: 'Such as like unto David of Old, desiring many wives and concubines, and also Solomon, his son.' Hardy's cross-references here are 2 Samuel 5:13 and 1 Kings 11:1-3, and they are the right two: the KJV joins concubines to wives in exactly one verse, 2 Samuel 5:13, which is David's, and the seven hundred wives of 1 Kings 11:3 are Solomon's. What the Book of Mormon supplies is the conjunction of the two under a single charge, which the KJV nowhere makes and which Deuteronomy 17:17 licenses.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 1.15 (2 Samuel 5:13; 1 Kings 11:1-3)
links.text: And David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron: and there were yet sons and daughters born to David.

pericopes.text: yea, and they also began to search much gold and silver, and began to be lifted up somewhat in pride;

provenance.other: “hardened in pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Daniel 5:20, which reads 'when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne'. That one verse contains both of the things Jacob 1:15-16 reports of the Nephites under their second king — a hardening and a lifting up in pride — in that order. “his heart was lifted up” occurs in exactly four KJV verses (2 Chronicles 17:6, 2 Chronicles 26:16, 2 Chronicles 32:25, Daniel 5:20), all of kings. “lifted up with pride” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:6, of a novice made an officer.
provenance.significance: Daniel 5:20 is the KJV's compressed account of what royal pride costs: Nebuchadnezzar's heart lifted up, his mind hardened in pride, deposed from his kingly throne. Jacob 1:15-16 narrates the same two motions in the same order under the reign of the second Nephite king, and Jacob 1:17 is the prophet arriving in the temple to preach against it — which is the office Daniel holds in his chapter. The alternative source is not idle either: 1 Timothy 3:6 warns against ordaining a novice 'lest being lifted up with pride he fall', and Jacob 1:18 is about who has been consecrated priest and by whose hand.
provenance.alternative: The vocabulary of a lifted-up heart is spread across four KJV verses and the whole prophetic idiom of pride; taken by itself 'lifted up somewhat in pride' identifies nothing. The case is the pairing with the hardening of 1:15.

links.note: 'They also began to search much gold and silver, and began to be lifted up somewhat in pride.' Read with 1:15's 'began to grow hard in their hearts', this is Daniel 5:20's two clauses in Daniel's order, and the KJV joins a hardening to a lifting-up in pride in that one verse only. Moderate: Jacob's preposition is 'in pride' where Daniel has 'in pride' of the mind and 1 Timothy 3:6 has 'with pride' of a man, and neither source is reproduced as a clause. The hardening at 1:15 is also doing double duty — it answers the 'harden not your hearts' of 1:7's Hebrews 3:8, and the chapter is arguably reporting the failure of its own opening warning.
links.text: But when his heart was lifted up, and his mind hardened in pride, he was deposed from his kingly throne, and they took his glory from him:

pericopes.text: wherefore, I, Jacob, gave unto them these words as I taught them in the temple, having firstly obtained mine errand from the Lord.
For I, Jacob, and my brother Joseph, had been consecrated priests, and teachers of this people, by the hand of Nephi.

And we did magnify our office unto the Lord, taking upon us the responsibility, answering the sins of the people upon our own heads, if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence; wherefore, by laboring with our mights, their blood might not come upon our garments; otherwise, their blood would come upon our garments, and we would not be found spotless at the last day.

provenance.other: “magnify mine office” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:13. “mine office” itself occurs in exactly two (Genesis 41:13, of Pharaoh's butler restored, and Romans 11:13), and only Paul magnifies one. Jacob 1:19 reads 'we did magnify our office unto the Lord', the singleton put into the first person plural.
provenance.significance: The clause Jacob borrows is the hinge of Romans 11: Paul magnifies his office as apostle to the Gentiles precisely in order to 'provoke to emulation them which are my flesh, and might save some of them' — the office is magnified toward the salvation of Israel, at the writer's own risk. Jacob magnifies his in the same shape and spells out the risk in the same sentence: the sins of the people come upon his own head if he does not teach them. Paul's next verses are the olive tree and the branches broken off, which is the figure Jacob 5 will take over whole and run for seventy-seven verses. The one Pauline clause about magnifying an office arrives in the Book of Mormon four chapters before the allegory that stands beside it in Romans.

links.note: 'And we did magnify our office unto the Lord, taking upon us the responsibility.' A three-word KJV singleton, moved from Paul's first person singular to the first person plural of Jacob and Joseph. The verb is not a general one in the KJV — what is usually magnified is the Lord, or his law, or his word — and an office is magnified in exactly one verse.
links.text: For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office:

provenance.route: Acts 18:6 + Acts 20:26, over Ezekiel 33:1-9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “our own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6 — 'Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean' — where it is 'your'. “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:26, Paul's farewell at Miletus: 'I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.' Jacob 1:19 has both halves of Paul's formula, the blood and the cleanness of the preacher, and takes the heads onto himself: the sins of the people come 'upon our own heads' if the teaching fails.
provenance.significance: The reversal is the finding. Paul says the blood is on THEIR heads and he is clean; Jacob says it will be on OURS if we do not teach. The Old Testament source behind Paul is the watchman of Ezekiel 33:6, whose failure to blow the trumpet makes him answerable — 'his blood will I require at the watchman's hand' — and Jacob has restored Ezekiel's liability to Paul's wording. What the two testaments hold apart, the verse fuses: Acts supplies the phrase, Ezekiel supplies the direction, and the result is a consecrated priest who is not clean by default.
provenance.alternative: The image of blood on a garment is also Isaiah 63:3 and Revelation 19:13, but those are the treader of the winepress and are stained on purpose; nothing in them concerns a teacher's liability.

links.note: 'Answering the sins of the people upon our own heads, if we did not teach them the word of God with all diligence; wherefore, by laboring with our mights, their blood might not come upon our garments.' Two KJV singletons stand behind the sentence, 'our own heads' at Acts 18:6 and 'pure from the blood' at Acts 20:26, both of them Paul disclaiming responsibility for hearers who would not listen. Jacob keeps the words and inverts the claim, which is Ezekiel 33:6's watchman rather than Paul's shaken raiment. The garments are Jacob's own contribution: no KJV verse puts a hearer's blood on a teacher's clothes.
links.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.other: “the sins of the people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 2:17: 'that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people'. Jacob 1:18-19 is about two men 'consecrated priests' who take the sins of the people upon their own heads.
provenance.significance: The one KJV verse that speaks of the sins of the people speaks of a high priest who bears them, and Jacob's sentence is written by a consecrated priest describing what he does with them. Read with the Hebrews 3 that governs Jacob 1:7, the borrowing is not isolated: Hebrews 2:17 is eight verses before 3:1's 'consider the Apostle and High Priest of our profession', and this chapter has already followed Hebrews 3 down to 3:18. The chapter's two ends, the exhortation at 1:7 and the priesthood at 1:19, are drawn from the same three columns of the epistle.
provenance.alternative: 'The sins of the people' is an obvious enough thing for a priest to say and the collocation is common in the Levitical vocabulary generally (Leviticus 4:3, 'the sin of the people'); the singleton is a fact about the exact string, not about the idea.

links.note: 'Answering the sins of the people upon our own heads.' The phrase occurs in exactly one KJV verse and that verse defines the office Jacob 1:18 has just claimed. Catalogued as an echo, not an allusion: four words shared, no syntax carried over, and the case rests on the coincidence of the wording with the priesthood the previous verse establishes and with the run through Hebrews 3 that the chapter has already made at 1:7.
links.text: Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God, to make reconciliation for the sins of the people.

provenance.other: “be found of him in peace” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 3:14, which continues 'without spot, and blameless' — the KJV's one place where being FOUND and being without spot are joined, and where the finding is eschatological (the verse before it is the new heavens and new earth). Jacob 1:19 reads 'we would not be found spotless at the last day'. “at the last day” occurs in exactly five KJV verses, all of them in John (6:39, 6:40, 6:44, 6:54, 11:24), so the temporal clause is Johannine and the spotlessness is Petrine.
provenance.significance: Jacob's closing clause is a composite of the two KJV idioms for the end: John's day on which the dead are raised, and Peter's inspection at which the diligent are found without spot. What Peter asks of every reader — 'be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot' — Jacob makes conditional on an office: he will be found spotless only if he has taught with diligence, and the same word does the work in both. Jude 1:23's 'garment spotted by the flesh' stands behind the metaphor's other half, since Jacob's spot is on a garment stained by someone else's blood.

links.note: 'Otherwise, their blood would come upon our garments, and we would not be found spotless at the last day.' Two KJV formulas are welded here: 'found … without spot' from 2 Peter 3:14, the only verse joining them, and 'at the last day', which occurs in exactly five KJV verses and all of them are John's. Moderate, and an echo rather than an allusion, because neither phrase is reproduced intact — 'found spotless' compresses Peter's three words into one.
links.text: Wherefore, beloved, seeing that ye look for such things, be diligent that ye may be found of him in peace, without spot, and blameless.

pericopes.text: The words which Jacob, the brother of Nephi, spake unto the people of Nephi, after the death of Nephi:

Now, my be loved brethren, I, Jacob, according to the responsibility which I am under to God, to magnify mine office with soberness, and that I might rid my garments of your sins, I come up into the temple this day, that I might declare unto you the word of God;

links.text: For I speak to you Gentiles, inasmuch as I am the apostle of the Gentiles, I magnify mine office:

provenance.other: “magnify mine office” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:13. The KJV magnifies the LORD, his word, his law and his name dozens of times; it magnifies an office once.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing gains an edge the sentence does not state. Paul magnifies his office in the middle of the olive-tree argument, and four sentences later warns the grafted branches, “Be not highminded, but fear” (Romans 11:20) — which is the whole burden of Jacob's next twenty verses against a people lifted up in the pride of their hearts. Jacob claims Paul's warrant for speaking and then delivers Paul's warning to the branches that were grafted in and grew proud.

links.note: “According to the responsibility which I am under to God, to magnify mine office with soberness.” The phrase is Paul's and only Paul's in the KJV, and Jacob has kept the first-person possessive that makes it a claim about the speaker's own standing rather than a doxology. “With soberness” pulls in the register of the Pastorals (“sober”, “sobriety”, 1 Timothy 2:9, 3:2) that this chapter will draw on again at 2:13 and 2:27 — so the sermon opens by describing its own authority in the vocabulary of the Pauline letters about church office.

links.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean; from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.

provenance.route: Acts 18:6 (with Acts 20:26) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “Your blood be upon your own heads” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 18:6, and “pure from the blood” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 20:26. Both are Paul discharging his liability for the people he has preached to; the watchman rule they enact is Ezekiel 33:8.
provenance.significance: Jacob's clause is the Acts image with one substitution. Paul shakes his *raiment* clean of the blood of those who will not hear; Jacob rids his *garments* of their sins. The image only works if guilt is a stain that transfers to the preacher's clothes when he stays silent — the watchman logic of Ezekiel 33 — and the KJV stages that logic exactly twice, both times in Paul's mouth. Note what follows in Acts 18:6: “from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.” The preacher who cleans his garments does so on his way out, which is not what Jacob is doing; he is cleaning them on his way *in*, at the temple door, before he speaks.

links.note: “That I might rid my garments of your sins, I come up into the temple this day.” The KJV has no verse about garments and sin together in this sense, so the clause is a fusion rather than a quotation: the raiment of Acts 18:6, the blood-guilt release of Acts 20:26, and the watchman's liability of Ezekiel 33:8. What makes the row worth writing is that Jacob puts the disclaimer at the start of the sermon and repeats the verb at 2:16 (“O that he would rid you from this iniquity”), where “rid you” is Exodus 6:6's phrase — so the chapter's opening and its central plea run on the same word doing two different scriptural jobs.

pericopes.text: and ye yourselves know, that I have hitherto been diligent in the office of my calling; but I this day am weighed down with much more desire and anxiety for the welfare of your souls, than I have hitherto been.
For behold, as yet, ye have been obedient unto the word of the Lord, which I have given unto you.

But behold, hearken ye unto me, and know that by the help of the All-powerful Creator of Heaven and Earth, I can tell you concerning your thoughts, how that ye are beginning to labor in sin, which sin appeareth very abominable unto me, yea, and abominable unto God.
Yea, it grieveth my soul and causeth me to shrink with shame before the presence of my Maker, that I might testify unto you concerning the wickedness of your hearts;

links.text: Now unto him that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy,

provenance.other: “before the presence of” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jude 1:24. The KJV's ordinary idioms are “in the presence of” and “from the presence of”; the doubled locative of Jude's benediction is unique to it.
provenance.significance: The echo runs backwards, and that is the interest. Jude's clause is the most confident sentence in the New Testament about standing before God — presented faultless, with exceeding joy. Jacob takes its one distinctive preposition-string and fills it with the opposite affect: he shrinks with shame. If the echo is real, the preacher who must accuse his congregation has borrowed the language of the doxology that promises they will be presented blameless, and inverted it against himself.

links.note: “It grieveth my soul and causeth me to shrink with shame before the presence of my Maker.” The verbal contact is a four-word string, which is thin — but the string is a KJV singleton, and the setting (a speaker's own standing before God, at the head of an address) is Jude's setting too. “My Maker” is Joban (Job 32:22, 35:10, 36:3), so the sentence is not straightforwardly Jude's; the row records the one phrase that is.
links.whyNot: Four words with no content word among them, and “before the presence of” could be assembled from KJV idiom without Jude in view. A reader who declines this row is not being unreasonable; it is kept because the string is a singleton and because the inversion, if intended, is worth having on the record.

pericopes.text: and also, it grieveth me that I must use so much boldness of speech, concerning you, before your wives and your children, many of whose feelings are exceeding tender, and chaste, and delicate before God, which thing is pleasing unto God;
and it supposeth me that they have come up hither to hear the pleasing word of God, yea, the word which healeth the wounded soul.

links.text: He healeth the broken in heart, and bindeth up their wounds.

provenance.other: “healeth the broken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 147:3. It is also the only KJV verse that holds healing, a broken heart and the binding of wounds in a single sentence — which is the exact set of images Jacob 2:8-10 works with.
provenance.significance: Psalm 147:3 is the sentence Jacob's whole exordium is arguing against himself with. The psalm says God heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds; Jacob says he has been commanded to do the reverse — “to enlarge the wounds of those which are already wounded, instead of consoling and healing their wounds” (2:9). He then names his audience at 2:10 as “the pure in heart, and the broken heart”, which is the psalm's category. The chapter's opening pathos is therefore not free-floating: it is a prophet apologising for having to violate Psalm 147:3, and the apology is worded out of the verse it violates.

links.note: “The pleasing word of God, yea, the word which healeth the wounded soul.” Healing, wounds and a broken heart appear together in the KJV once, and Jacob 2:8-10 uses all three in three consecutive verses, in the psalm's order — heal, wound, broken heart. 2:9's “instead of consoling and healing their wounds” is the psalm's second clause negated. The link is catalogued at 2:8 where the vocabulary enters and governs the paragraph through 2:10.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, it burdeneth my soul, that I should be constrained because of the strict commandment which I have received from God, to admonish you, according to your crimes, to enlarge the wounds of those which are already wounded, instead of consoling and healing their wounds; and those which have not been wounded, instead of feasting upon the pleasing word of God, have daggers placed to pierce their souls, and wound their delicate minds.

links.text: There is that speaketh like the piercings of a sword: but the tongue of the wise is health.

provenance.other: “the piercings of a sword” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 12:18. It is the KJV's only image of speech as a stabbing weapon.
provenance.significance: Proverbs 12:18 is built on precisely the antithesis Jacob 2:8-9 is built on: words that pierce like a blade against words that are health. Jacob has taken both halves and assigned them to the same speaker — he is the tongue that should be health (2:8, “the word which healeth the wounded soul”) and is compelled to be the sword instead. The proverb's two clauses become the two things one sermon does to two halves of one congregation.

links.note: “Have daggers placed to pierce their souls, and wound their delicate minds.” The KJV never says “dagger”, so the noun is the Book of Mormon's own; what is borrowed is the figure. Proverbs 12:18 is its only KJV source, and it supplies not just the piercing but the healing that Jacob 2:8 has just used as its opposite. That both halves of a single proverb appear in two consecutive verses, in order, is what carries the row above the level of a shared metaphor.

pericopes.text: But, notwithstanding the greatness of the task, I must do according to the strict commands of God, and tell you concerning your wickedness and abominations, in the presence of the pure in heart, and the broken heart, and under the glance of the piercing eye of the Almighty God.

links.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.

provenance.other: “the pure in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:8. Psalm 24:4 has “a pure heart” and Psalm 73:1 “such as are of a clean heart”, neither of which is this substantive plural.
provenance.significance: Jacob 2 draws on the Sermon on the Mount twice, and both times it takes a sentence about who is blessed and turns it into a description of who is in the room. Here the beatitude's promise — they shall see God — is replaced by the Almighty's “piercing eye” seeing them; at 2:18 the Sermon's command to seek the kingdom first becomes the chapter's economic rule. The Sermon is functioning as this sermon's model, which is a reasonable thing for a temple discourse to do and an anachronistic thing for a sixth-century BC one.

links.note: “In the presence of the pure in heart, and the broken heart, and under the glance of the piercing eye of the Almighty God.” The beatitude's exact substantive stands as a name for part of the congregation. Set beside “the broken heart” — Psalm 34:18's phrase, likewise a KJV singleton — the verse names its audience with two scriptural categories in a row, one from the Psalter and one from Matthew 5.

links.text: The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.

provenance.route: Psalm 34:18 (with Psalm 51:17) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “broken heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 34:18; “a broken and a contrite heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 51:17. The commoner KJV forms are “broken in heart” (Psalm 147:3) and “brokenhearted” (Isaiah 61:1).
provenance.significance: The psalm's point is consolation: the LORD is *nigh* to the broken heart. Jacob puts the broken heart in the room and then, thirty-three verses later, tells the men in front of him that they made it — “Ye have broken the hearts of your tender wives” (2:35). The category the psalm exists to comfort is, by the end of the chapter, a category this congregation manufactured. Nothing in either text says so; the repetition of the phrase says it.

links.note: The exact string is the Psalter's and appears once there. In a chapter that will end by charging its hearers with breaking hearts, naming the broken-hearted as present at the outset is structural rather than decorative, and the borrowed phrase is what makes the structure visible.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, I must tell you the truth, according to the plainness of the word of God. For behold, as I inquired of the Lord, thus came the word unto me, saying, Jacob, get thou up into the temple on the morrow, and declare the word which I shall give thee, unto this people.

And now behold, my brethren, this is the word which I declare unto you, that many of you have began to search for gold, and for silver, and all manner of precious ores, in the which this land, which is a land of promise unto you, and to your seed, doth abound most plentifully.

And the hand of Providence hath smiled upon you most pleasingly, that you have obtained many riches; and because that some of you have obtained more abundantly than that of your brethren, ye are lifted up in the pride of your hearts, and wear stiff necks, and high heads, because of the costliness of your apparel, and persecute your brethren, because that ye suppose that ye are better then they.

links.text: In like manner also, that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefacedness and sobriety; not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly array;

provenance.route: 1 Timothy 2:9 (with Revelation 18:19) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “costly array” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 2:9, and “costliness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 18:19. Jacob's “costliness of your apparel” is the noun of the one verse fitted to the subject of the other.
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 2:9 forbids costly array to *women*; Jacob 2:13 charges it against *men*, and the chapter's women are its victims rather than its offenders throughout (2:7, 2:31-35). The reversal is deliberate enough to be worth stating: the Book of Mormon has taken the New Testament's standard text on ostentatious dress, moved it off the women it was written against, and used it to indict the husbands. Revelation 18:19 supplies the abstract noun, and with it the merchants of Babylon weeping over the wealth that made them rich — the frame in which costliness is a thing that gets destroyed.

links.note: “Ye are lifted up in the pride of your hearts, and wear stiff necks, and high heads, because of the costliness of your apparel.” Two KJV singletons meet in one clause: the adjective-phrase of 1 Timothy 2:9 and the noun of Revelation 18:19, both attached to “apparel”, which is 1 Timothy 2:9's word as well. The pride-of-heart formula behind the first half is Obadiah 1:3 and Jeremiah 49:16 (“the pride of thine heart” occurs in exactly two KJV verses), and “stiff neck” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 31:27 and Psalm 75:5 — the latter in the company of “Lift not up your horn on high”, which is close to Jacob's “high heads”.

links.text: Moreover the LORD saith, Because the daughters of Zion are haughty, and walk with stretched forth necks and wanton eyes, walking and mincing as they go, and making a tinkling with their feet:

provenance.other: “stretched forth necks” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “are haughty” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Isaiah 3:16. Isaiah 3:18-23 then runs the KJV's longest inventory of costly apparel.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 3:16-24 is the Bible's set piece on proud necks and expensive clothes, and Jacob 2:13 has the neck, the height and the costly apparel in one sentence. But Isaiah indicts the daughters of Zion, and Jacob indicts the men — and then, at 2:31-33, gives the daughters the tears Isaiah 3:26 gives to a mourning city. The chapter appears to have taken Isaiah 3 apart and re-dealt it: the sin to the husbands, the lamentation to the wives.

links.note: The verbal contact is at the level of image rather than string — Jacob writes “stiff necks, and high heads”, not Isaiah's “stretched forth necks” — so this is filed as an echo, not an allusion. It is worth recording because Isaiah 3 is the one KJV passage that puts a proud neck and a wardrobe in the same oracle, because 2 Nephi has already transcribed Isaiah 3 in full at 2 Nephi 13, and because the chapter's redistribution of Isaiah's roles between husbands and wives is a finding the wording alone would not yield.
links.whyNot: No phrase of Isaiah 3:16 survives into Jacob 2:13 intact; the shared material is a neck, a height and a wardrobe, all of which the chapter could have reached independently. 1 Timothy 2:9 is the demonstrable source for the apparel clause, and this row is an additional background, not a competitor to it.

pericopes.text: And now my brethren, do ye suppose that God justifieth you in this thing? Behold, I say unto you, Nay. But he condemneth you, and if ye persist in these things, his judgments must speedily come unto you.

links.text: Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth.

provenance.other: “It is God that justifieth” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 8:33, and the sentence immediately following it is “Who is he that condemneth?” Romans 8:33-34 is the only place in the KJV where God's justifying and the question of condemnation stand in successive clauses.
provenance.significance: Jacob asks Romans' question and refuses Romans' answer. Paul's rhetorical pair is a guarantee — God justifies, therefore no one condemns; Jacob puts the same pair to his congregation as a question they have evidently been answering wrongly, and breaks it: “do ye suppose that God justifieth you in this thing? … Nay. But he condemneth you.” If the borrowing is real, this is a verse of the Book of Mormon quoting Romans 8 in order to deny that it applies, which is a more interesting relation to a New Testament text than agreement would be.

links.note: “Do ye suppose that God justifieth you in this thing? Behold, I say unto you, Nay. But he condemneth you.” The two verbs are Romans 8:33-34's two verbs, in Romans' order, and “justify” as something God does to a person is a Pauline construction the Old Testament does not supply in this form. The Book of Mormon has kept the pair and reversed the verdict. Note that Jacob 2:2 has already borrowed from Romans 11:13, so the chapter reaches Romans twice.

pericopes.text: O that he would shew you that he can pierce you, and with one glance of his eye, he can smite you to the dust.
O that he would rid you from this iniquity, and abomination. And, O that ye would listen unto the word of his commands, and let not this pride of your hearts destroy your souls.

links.text: Wherefore say unto the children of Israel, I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will rid you out of their bondage, and I will redeem you with a stretched out arm, and with great judgments:

provenance.other: “rid you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Exodus 6:6. The verb is common enough in the KJV, but God ridding a people is this verse alone.
provenance.significance: Exodus 6:6 governs two verses of this chapter, nine apart. At 2:16 Jacob asks God to “rid you from this iniquity”, using the verb of the deliverance oracle; at 2:25 God says he “led this people forth out of the land of Jerusalem, by the power of mine arm”, which is Exodus 6:6's second clause with Jerusalem substituted for Egypt. Recover the source and the substitution is the argument: the people who were brought out by the outstretched arm are told that the bondage they now need ridding of is their own iniquity, and that the exodus which brought them here was for the purpose of raising a righteous branch (2:25), not for enriching them.

links.note: “O that he would rid you from this iniquity, and abomination.” The phrase is the deliverance formula of Exodus 6:6 turned inward — the same verb, the same divine subject, the same construction of a people needing to be got out of something, with iniquity in the place of Egyptian bondage. The formulaic “O that ye would” of 2:16's second clause is Job 13:5's, and carries no weight; the “rid you” does. Filed as moderate because a single verb, however rare in this application, is a narrow base — but see 2:25, where the rest of Exodus 6:6 reappears.

pericopes.text: Think of your brethren, like unto yourselves, and be familiar with all, and free with your substance, that they may be rich like unto you.

links.text: But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality:

provenance.other: “there may be equality” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 8:14. No KJV verse contains Jacob's clause “that they may be rich like unto you”, but 2 Corinthians 8:9 has “that ye through his poverty might be rich”, the KJV's nearest sentence of the kind.
provenance.significance: 2 Corinthians 8 is the New Testament's argument that the surplus of one congregation exists to fill the want of another, and that the goal is parity rather than charity. Jacob 2:17 states the same doctrine in the same order — think of the brethren as like yourselves, be free with your substance, until they are as rich as you are — and it is the only place in this chapter where the remedy for wealth is redistribution rather than repentance.

links.note: “Be familiar with all, and free with your substance, that they may be rich like unto you.” No string is reproduced, so the row is conceptual and moderate. What earns it is the shape of the claim: parity, not almsgiving, as the object of giving, which in the KJV is 2 Corinthians 8's distinctive teaching and is stated nowhere in the Old Testament. Jacob's added premise — “think of your brethren, like unto yourselves” — is the equality clause turned into a mental discipline.
links.whyNot: Verbal contact is close to nil, and a preacher arguing for generosity could reach “that they may be rich like unto you” without Paul. A reader who wants a string will not find one here.

pericopes.text: But before ye seek for riches, seek ye for the Kingdom of God.

links.text: But seek ye first the kingdom of God, and his righteousness; and all these things shall be added unto you.

provenance.route: Matthew 6:33 or Luke 12:31 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “seek ye first the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 6:33, and “seek ye the kingdom” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 12:31. Both are introduced by “But”, and both are followed by the promise that the other things will be added.
provenance.significance: Jacob 2:18-19 does not merely quote the saying, it *operationalises* it. Matthew and Luke both promise that the other things will be added; Jacob says what the other things are (riches), states the condition on which they may be sought (after a hope in Christ), and then licenses the seeking on the terms of Matthew 25 — to clothe the naked and feed the hungry. The sermon has read the Sermon's promise as an economic rule with an order of operations, and 2:19 is the rule's second clause.

links.note: “But before ye seek for riches, seek ye for the Kingdom of God.” Mediation test run on Matthew 6:33 against Luke 12:31 (tools/mediation-check.py): **no decisive divergence** — Jacob reproduces neither Matthew's “first” nor Luke's “rather”, and neither “and his righteousness” nor “all these things shall be added unto you”. What can be said is that Jacob's shorter object-phrase matches Luke's shorter form, while the priority Matthew's “first” asserts is what Jacob's “before ye seek for riches” restates in its own words. The row is therefore direct-NT with the synoptic form left open, and the case for dependence rests on the phrase plus the adversative “But” that both gospels share. Note that Matthew 5:8 has already been used at 2:10.

pericopes.text: And after that ye have obtained a hope in Christ, ye shall obtain riches, if ye seek them; and ye will seek them, for the intent to do good; to clothe the naked, and to feed the hungry, and to liberate the captive, and administer relief to the sick, and the afflicted.

links.text: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me.

provenance.route: Matthew 25:35-36 (with Isaiah 58:6-7) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The four objects of Jacob's list — the naked, the hungry, the captive, the sick — are Matthew 25:35-36's list minus the stranger and with the prisoner rendered as a captive to be liberated. “I was sick” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:36, which is the only KJV verse to name the sick among the objects of mercy in such a list. Isaiah 58:6-7 supplies the same set in the Old Testament — “deal thy bread to the hungry” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — but has no sick.
provenance.significance: The works of mercy in the KJV come in two canonical lists, Isaiah 58:6-7 and Matthew 25:35-36, and Jacob's has one item each list lacks: the sick (Matthew only) and the liberated captive (Isaiah only, and Luke 4:18). So the verse is a fusion of the two, which is what a reader working from a whole English Bible would produce and not what either source alone would. Set that beside 2:18: the Sermon on the Mount licenses the seeking, and the judgment of the sheep and the goats specifies what the money is for — the two Matthean passages about wealth, in order.

links.note: “Ye will seek them, for the intent to do good; to clothe the naked, and to feed the hungry, and to liberate the captive, and administer relief to the sick, and the afflicted.” No single clause is reproduced, but the list is. A mediation test on Isaiah 61:1 against Luke 4:18 for the captive was run and returned no decisive divergence — Jacob's “liberate” is neither Isaiah's “proclaim liberty” nor Luke's “preach deliverance”, and both source texts are about proclamation rather than release, so neither can be shown to be in view for that item specifically. What the row claims is the composite list, not any one phrase in it.

links.text: That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate;

provenance.other: Four KJV singletons stand in nine verses of 1 Timothy 6 and all four bear on Jacob 2:13-19: “will be rich” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (6:9), “love of money” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (6:10), “uncertain riches” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (6:17), and “rich in good works” and “ready to distribute” each occur in exactly one KJV verse (6:18).
provenance.significance: 1 Timothy 6:9-18 is the New Testament's most complete treatment of what to do about a rich congregation, and it runs in the order Jacob 2 runs: those who *will* be rich fall into a snare (6:9 / Jacob 2:12-14), the rich are not to be highminded (6:17 / Jacob 2:13, “lifted up in the pride of your hearts”), and yet they are not told to divest but to be rich in good works and ready to distribute (6:18 / Jacob 2:17-19). Jacob's much-quoted resolution — riches are permitted to those who will seek them “for the intent to do good” — is 1 Timothy 6:18's first clause, “that they do good”, converted into a condition. The same chapter also supplies the vocabulary Jacob 2:2 borrowed from Romans 11 and the “apparel” of 1 Timothy 2:9 at 2:13, so the Pastorals stand behind this sermon at three separate points.

links.note: “And ye will seek them, for the intent to do good.” The clause that makes Jacob 2 a text about stewardship rather than renunciation reproduces the purpose-clause of 1 Timothy 6:18. Read the two paragraphs side by side and the correspondence is sequential, not incidental: the danger of wanting to be rich, the charge against being highminded, and then the permission — good works and readiness to distribute — in the same order in both. The KJV has no Old Testament passage that arranges the argument this way.

pericopes.text: And now my brethren, I have spoken unto you concerning pride; and those of you which have afflicted your neighbor, and persecuted him, because that ye were proud in your hearts, of the things which God hath given you, what say ye of it?

Do ye not suppose that such things are abominable unto him, who created all flesh? And the one being is as precious in his sight as the other. And all flesh is of the dust; and for the self same end hath he created them, that they should keep his commandments, and glorify him forever.

links.text: All go unto one place; all are of the dust, and all turn to dust again.

provenance.other: “all are of the dust” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ecclesiastes 3:20. Genesis 3:19's “dust thou art” and Job 34:15's “man shall turn again unto dust” are the near neighbours, and neither has the plural universal.
provenance.significance: Ecclesiastes 3:20 makes its claim in order to level man with the beasts — the verse before it says they have all one breath, and that a man has no preeminence above a beast. Jacob uses the same sentence to level rich with poor: “the one being is as precious in his sight as the other. And all flesh is of the dust.” The Preacher's most deflating argument about human dignity is turned into an argument for equal dignity, which is a real reversal of the source's purpose. That Jacob's next clause is Ecclesiastes 12:13's conclusion — keep his commandments — suggests the whole book, not the single verse, was in view.

links.note: “And all flesh is of the dust; and for the self same end hath he created them, that they should keep his commandments, and glorify him forever.” The dust clause is Ecclesiastes 3:20's, and the commandment clause is Ecclesiastes 12:13's (“Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man”) — the book's premise and its conclusion, joined in one sentence, with Ecclesiastes' “whole duty of man” replaced by the created purpose. Filed moderate because “keep his commandments” occurs in eighteen KJV verses and cannot carry weight on its own; the dust clause is what identifies the source. The 1830 reads “self same”, two words, where 1920 prints “selfsame”.

pericopes.text: And now I make an end of speaking unto you concerning this pride. And were it not that I must speak unto you concerning a grosser crime my heart would rejoice excedingly, because of you.

But the word of God burthens me because of your grosser crimes. For behold, thus saith the Lord: This People begin to wax in iniquity; they understand not the Scriptures: for they seek to excuse themselves in committing whoredoms, because of the things which were written concerning David, and Solomon his Son.

links.text: Jesus answered and said unto them, Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.

provenance.other: “not knowing the scriptures” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 22:29 (Mark 12:24 reads “because ye know not the scriptures”). It is the KJV's only formulation of scriptural ignorance as the cause of a marriage error.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest borrowing and it is easy to miss. Matthew 22:23-30 is the one New Testament passage where a question about plural marriage is answered with the charge of not knowing the scriptures — the Sadducees' woman who had seven husbands, and Jesus's reply, “Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures, nor the power of God.” Jacob 2:23 brings exactly that charge (“they understand not the Scriptures”) against exactly that error (“they seek to excuse themselves in committing whoredoms, because of the things which were written concerning David, and Solomon”). Seven verses later, at 2:30, the chapter uses “raise up seed unto me”, which is the phrase from the Sadducees' question itself at Matthew 22:24. The Book of Mormon's law of one wife is framed, at both ends, in the language of the Gospel debate about serial marriage — and the accusation Jesus makes of the Sadducees is the accusation Jacob makes of the Nephites.

links.note: “This People begin to wax in iniquity; they understand not the Scriptures: for they seek to excuse themselves in committing whoredoms.” The charge is not a KJV commonplace: outside Matthew 22:29 and its Markan parallel, no KJV verse makes scriptural ignorance the ground of a marriage error. That Jacob's next mention of scripture is “the things which were written concerning David, and Solomon his son” — an appeal to Old Testament precedent to license plural marriage — makes the Matthean setting nearly exact, since the Sadducees' case is likewise an appeal to what Moses wrote about taking a brother's wife.

pericopes.text: Behold, David and Solomon truly had many wives and concubines, which thing was abominable before me, saith the Lord.

links.text: Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away: neither shall he greatly multiply to himself silver and gold.

provenance.other: “multiply wives” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Deuteronomy 17:17. It is also the only KJV verse that forbids accumulated wives and accumulated silver and gold in a single sentence.
provenance.significance: This is the structural key to the chapter, and it explains why one sermon holds two apparently unrelated subjects. Jacob 2 condemns, in order, the search for gold and silver (2:12-13) and the taking of many wives (2:23-24) — the two prohibitions of the law of the king, in one paragraph each. Deuteronomy 17:17 is the statute David and Solomon are conventionally read as having broken, and it is the answer to the objection Jacob's hearers are making: that scripture permits what David and Solomon did. It does not, and the verse that says so is the law governing kings. The Book of Mormon does not cite it. The whole architecture of the chapter is built on it.

links.note: “David and Solomon truly had many wives and concubines, which thing was abominable before me, saith the Lord.” The phrase “wives and concubines” appears in no KJV verse at all, so this is not a verbal borrowing; it is a link at the level of the argument. What makes it more than a topical coincidence is the pairing: the two things Deuteronomy 17:17 forbids a king are the two things Jacob 2 forbids his people, in one discourse, with the second introduced as the “grosser crime” (2:22) that the first has prepared. Kept at high confidence because the coincidence of both prohibitions, in one chapter, against the very kings the statute was framed for is not plausibly accidental — but marked `kjvSpecific: "no"`, since no English wording is at stake.

links.text: Did not Solomon king of Israel sin by these things? yet among many nations was there no king like him, who was beloved of his God, and God made him king over all Israel: nevertheless even him did outlandish women cause to sin.

provenance.route: Nehemiah 13:23-27 (with 1 Kings 11:1-3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “outlandish women” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 13:26. Nehemiah 13:23-27 is the only place in the KJV where Solomon's marriages are cited, in a sermon, as the precedent a later congregation is being warned by.
provenance.significance: Jacob's rhetorical situation has one precise biblical counterpart. Nehemiah, rebuking a congregation for its marriages, does not argue from statute but from Solomon: if the wisest king in Israel was brought to sin this way, what are you? Jacob does the same in reverse — his people are arguing *from* Solomon that the practice is licensed, and he answers that the record they cite is a record of abomination. Both preachers make the same move on the same king; they simply meet him coming from opposite directions.

links.note: “Because of the things which were written concerning David, and Solomon his son … which thing was abominable before me.” 1 Kings 11:3 supplies the count of wives and concubines; Nehemiah 13:26 supplies the homiletic use of it, which is what Jacob 2:23-24 is doing. Filed moderate: no phrase crosses over, and “Solomon his son” is a common KJV formula (1 Chronicles 29:28 among others), so the row rests on the parallel of rhetorical situation rather than on wording.
links.whyNot: Nothing verbal is shared. A reader could hold that Jacob needs only 1 Kings 11 and the general fact of Solomon's harem, with no particular sermon in view.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, thus saith the Lord: I have led this people forth out of the land of Jerusalem, by the power of mine arm, that I might raise up unto me a righteous branch, from the fruit of the loins of Joseph.

links.text: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will raise unto David a righteous Branch, and a King shall reign and prosper, and shall execute judgment and justice in the earth.

provenance.route: Jeremiah 23:5 (with Acts 2:30) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “righteous Branch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Jeremiah 23:5 (Jeremiah 33:15 reads “the Branch of righteousness”), and “fruit of his loins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 2:30. Both source verses are about David.
provenance.significance: The substitution is the finding. In the KJV the righteous Branch is raised *unto David*, and the fruit of the loins from which Christ comes is *David's* (Acts 2:30). Jacob 2:25 keeps both phrases and changes the name: the branch is raised “unto me”, and the loins are “the loins of Joseph”. This falls two verses before the chapter's denunciation of what was “written concerning David” — so the same paragraph that strips David of his precedent also strips him of his messianic phrase and gives it to Joseph. Neither text says the transfer is polemical. Their proximity says it.

links.note: “That I might raise up unto me a righteous branch, from the fruit of the loins of Joseph.” Two KJV singletons in one clause, both belonging in their sources to David, both reassigned. The verse's first half — “I have led this people forth out of the land of Jerusalem, by the power of mine arm” — is the exodus formula of Exodus 6:6 with Jerusalem for Egypt (see the link at 2:16), so the sentence carries a redemption clause and a messianic clause and reroutes both away from Egypt and away from David.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, I, the Lord God, will not suffer that this people shall do like unto them of old.
Wherefore, my brethren, hear me, and hearken to the word of the Lord: for there shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none:

links.text: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;

provenance.route: 1 Timothy 3:2 (with 3:12, Titus 1:6) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “one wife” occurs in exactly three KJV verses — 1 Timothy 3:2, 1 Timothy 3:12 and Titus 1:6 — and “the husband of one wife” occurs in exactly two KJV verses. All are Pastoral Epistles, and all are qualifications for church office.
provenance.significance: Monogamy stated as a numerical rule is, in the King James Bible, a Pastoral-Epistle idea and nowhere else's. Genesis 2:24 argues one flesh, not one wife; the Torah regulates plural marriage rather than forbidding it. So when Jacob 2:27 legislates that no man “have save it be one wife”, the English it legislates in belongs to the three verses that set the marital qualification for bishops and deacons — a rule for officers, generalised here to a whole people. That generalisation is the chapter's actual innovation, and it is made in borrowed words.

links.note: “There shall not any man among you have save it be one wife; and concubines he shall have none.” Mediation test run on the Genesis 2:24 cluster (tools/mediation-check.py, Genesis 2:24 against Matthew 19:5 and against 1 Corinthians 6:16): **no decisive divergence, because Jacob reproduces none of the shared wording at all** — no “leave his father and his mother”, no “cleave”, no “one flesh”, no “twain”. The one-flesh tradition is therefore not the source of this verse, however natural an expectation it is (see the exclusion filed at 2:27), and the Pastorals are. Filed moderate rather than high because two of the three words are among the commonest in English and the phrase could in principle be assembled independently; what argues against that is that the KJV itself never assembles it except in the Pastorals.

pericopes.text: For I, the Lord God, delighteth in the chastity of women. And whoredoms is an abomination before me: thus saith the Lord of Hosts.
Wherefore, this peeple shall keep my commandments, saith the Lord of Hosts, or cursed be the land for their sakes.

links.text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

provenance.other: “cursed is the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:17. Genesis 8:21's “I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake” is its only close relative, and it is a promise not to repeat it.
provenance.significance: The curse of Genesis 3:17 is passed on a man who listened to his wife and is enacted on the ground he must work. Jacob 2:29 threatens the same curse on the same terms against men who have not listened to their wives at all — whose wives, in the next six verses, are shown sorrowing and mourning. Recover the source and the sentence carries an irony the chapter does not spell out: the archetypal marital sin the Bible curses the land for is a husband deferring to his wife, and the sin Jacob curses the land for is a husband disregarding her.

links.note: “Wherefore, this peeple shall keep my commandments, saith the Lord of Hosts, or cursed be the land for their sakes.” The construction — a curse on the land, given “for” the sake of the offenders — reproduces Genesis 3:17's clause with “land” for “ground” and a plural possessive. The 1830 spelling “peeple” is a compositor's, not evidentially significant. The threat is conditional in a way Genesis is not, which is why this is filed as an allusion rather than a quotation.

pericopes.text: For if I will, saith the Lord of Hosts, raise up seed unto me, I will command my people: otherwise, they shall hearken unto these things.

links.text: Saying, Master, Moses said, If a man die, having no children, his brother shall marry his wife, and raise up seed unto his brother.

provenance.route: Genesis 38:8 via Matthew 22:24 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “raise up seed” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Genesis 38:8, Matthew 22:24, Mark 12:19 and Luke 20:28. Genesis reads “raise up seed **to** thy brother”; all three synoptics read “raise up seed **unto** his brother”. Jacob 2:30 reads “raise up seed **unto** me”.
provenance.significance: The preposition decides it, and it decides in favour of the Gospels. mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence, because the tool sets aside single common words and the possessive necessarily differs — God is speaking of himself, so neither “thy brother” nor “his brother” could stand. But the one word the two forms genuinely differ on that Jacob could reproduce is the preposition, and Jacob has the New Testament's. The point matters because of where the phrase sits: it is the exception clause to the law of one wife, and it is worded out of the Sadducees' question about a woman with seven husbands — the same pericope Jacob 2:23 drew “not knowing the scriptures” from, seven verses earlier.

links.note: “For if I will, saith the Lord of Hosts, raise up seed unto me, I will command my people.” The levirate formula is transferred from a brother to God, which is a striking reassignment: the clause that in scripture licenses one man taking another's wife becomes the clause that licenses God suspending the law of one wife. Filed moderate because a single preposition is a narrow base for the mediation call — but it is the only point at which the Genesis and Gospel forms differ in a way this verse could register, and the chapter's independent use of Matthew 22:29 at 2:23 makes the Gospel pericope demonstrably present to it.
links.whyNot: The mediation rests on “unto” against “to”, one word, and the tool declined to score it. A reader who thinks Genesis 38:8 is the source and the preposition drift accidental has a defensible position; what would be hard to explain on that view is Jacob 2:23's use of Matthew 22:29 from the same passage.

pericopes.text: For behold, I, the Lord, have seen the sorrow, and heard the mourning of the daughters of my people, in the land of Jerusalem; yea, and in all the lands of my people, because of the wickedness and abominations of their husbands.

links.text: And the LORD said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows;

provenance.route: Exodus 3:7 (with Exodus 2:23-25) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “seen the affliction” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Exodus 3:7 and its citation at Acts 7:34, and “heard their cry” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which Exodus 3:7 is the first. The doubled formula — I have seen X of my people, and heard Y — is Exodus 3:7's alone.
provenance.significance: Jacob 2:31 is the call of Moses with the oppressor changed. Exodus 3:7 has God seeing the affliction of his people in Egypt and hearing their cry against their taskmasters; Jacob 2:31 has God seeing the sorrow and hearing the mourning of the daughters of his people “because of the wickedness and abominations of their husbands”. The husbands stand where Pharaoh's taskmasters stand. This is the chapter's most consequential figural move — the men who were brought out of bondage (2:25, and see Exodus 6:6 at 2:16) are told in the language of the exodus that they have become the Egyptians — and the whole of 2:32-33, with the cries coming up and the threat of a visitation, follows the Exodus 2:23-3:9 sequence in order.

links.note: “I, the Lord, have seen the sorrow, and heard the mourning of the daughters of my people.” The verbs, their order, the possessive “my people”, and the causal clause naming the oppressor are all Exodus 3:7's; “sorrow” is that verse's third element (“I know their sorrows”) promoted into the first clause. That the daughters are the sufferers and their own husbands the taskmasters is the substitution the source makes legible.

pericopes.text: And I will not suffer, saith the Lord of Hosts, that the cries of the fair daughters of this people, which I have led out of the land of Jerusalem, shall come up unto me, against the men of my people, saith the Lord of Hosts;

links.text: Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.

provenance.other: “the cries of them” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “are entered into the ears” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both James 5:4. “Lord of sabaoth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, James 5:4 and Romans 9:29; the KJV's ordinary rendering of the same title, and the one Jacob uses six times in this chapter, is “Lord of hosts”.
provenance.significance: James 5:1-6 is the New Testament's denunciation of a rich congregation, and it contains, in four verses, everything Jacob 2 has been doing: weep and howl, ye rich men (5:1); your riches are corrupted and your garments motheaten (5:2, against Jacob 2:13's costly apparel); the cries of the defrauded entering the ears of the Lord of sabaoth (5:4).
