Jacob 2:32 has the cries, the coming up to God, and the divine title — in the Old Testament form, “Lord of Hosts”, which is what James 5:4's “sabaoth” transliterates. And the epistle's author is, in Greek, Iakobos: James is Jacob. The one biblical letter that bears this prophet's name is the one that argues his sermon, and the catalogue can record the coincidence without deciding what to make of it.

links.note: “I will not suffer … that the cries of the fair daughters of this people … shall come up unto me, against the men of my people, saith the Lord of Hosts.” Two KJV singletons stand in James 5:4 and both concern cries reaching God against the men who wronged the crier. Jacob substitutes the ascent-formula of Exodus 2:23 (“their cry came up unto God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse) for James's “entered into the ears”, so the row is a fusion rather than a quotation — but the situation, the title, and the direction of the cry are James's, and the chapter's riches material at 2:12-13 has already been standing on the same page of the epistle.

pericopes.text: for they shall not lead away captive, the daughters of my people, because of their tenderness, save I shall visit them with a sore curse, even unto destruction: for they shall not commit whoredoms, like unto they of old, saith the Lord of Hosts.

And now behold, my brethren, ye know that these commandments were given to our father Lehi; wherefore, ye have known them before; and ye have come unto great condemnation; for ye have done these things, which ye ought not to have done.

Behold, ye have done greater iniquities than the Lamanites, our brethren. Ye have broken the hearts of your tender wives, and lost the confidence of your children, because of your bad examples before them; and the sobbings of their hearts ascendeth up to God against you. And because of the strictness of the word of God, which cometh down against you, many hearts died, pierced with deep wounds.

links.text: Reproach hath broken my heart; and I am full of heaviness: and I looked for some to take pity, but there was none; and for comforters, but I found none.

provenance.route: Psalm 69:20 (with Psalm 147:3) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “broken my heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 69:20, and it is the KJV's only instance of a heart broken by another party's conduct rather than described as a state. “healeth the broken” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 147:3.
provenance.significance: The chapter closes on the Psalter it opened with. At 2:8-10 Jacob describes his own commission against Psalm 147:3 — he must wound where God heals — and names “the broken heart” among his hearers (Psalm 34:18). At 2:35 he tells the men that they are the ones who broke those hearts. Psalm 69:20 supplies the transitive form and, with it, the sufferer's complaint that no comforter came; Jacob's wives are given the same silence, and the sobbing that goes up to God in the next clause is what fills it.

links.note: “Ye have broken the hearts of your tender wives, and lost the confidence of your children … and the sobbings of their hearts ascendeth up to God against you.” The transitive “broken … hearts” is Psalm 69:20's construction, and the ascent-clause is Exodus 2:23's (“their cry came up unto God” occurs in exactly one KJV verse), continuing the exodus frame of 2:31-32 — the sobbing of wives now doing what the groaning of Israel in Egypt did. The 1830's “ascendeth up” was corrected to “ascend” in 1920; the singular verb with a plural subject is the sort of concord the later edition smoothed, and the first edition preserves it. (The dossier's report of 1830 “confidence” → 1920 “confldence” is a typesetting artefact in the collation, not a real variant.)

pericopes.text: But behold, I, Jacob, would speak unto you that are pure in heart. Look unto God with firmness of mind, and pray unto him with exceeding faith, and he will console you in your afflictions, and he will plead your cause, and send down justice upon those who seek your destruction.

provenance.other: “pure in heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:8. The Psalter has the idea but not the phrase — Psalm 24:4 reads “clean hands, and a pure heart”, Psalm 73:1 “of a clean heart”, Psalm 51:10 “Create in me a clean heart”. The exact English construction is the Beatitude's.
provenance.significance: Jacob does with the sixth Beatitude what Luke 6 does with the whole set: he states it, and then turns it over into a woe. 3:1 addresses those who are pure in heart and promises consolation; 3:3 opens “But, wo, wo, unto you that are not pure in heart”. Recover Matthew 5:8's second half — “for they shall see God” — and the sermon's arc appears: the beatitude's reward is sight of God, and Jacob's threat five verses later is that his hearers will be “brought with them before the throne of God” and be the darker party there. What the Beatitude offers as blessing, Jacob holds out as exposure.

links.note: “I, Jacob, would speak unto you that are pure in heart.” The phrase is a KJV singleton and it organizes the whole opening of the chapter, appearing three times in three verses (3:1, 3:2, 3:3) and supplying the hinge on which the sermon turns from consolation to woe. Jacob's chapter also picks up the Sermon's other governing verb at 3:9, where the commandment is that ye “revile no more” — Matthew 5:11 is the KJV verse that makes reviling the disciple's expected lot, three verses below the one Jacob starts from. Well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold for a quotation, and catalogued as allusion accordingly.
links.text: Blessed are the pure in heart: for they shall see God.

provenance.alternative: “plead my cause” occurs in exactly five KJV verses (1 Samuel 24:15, Psalm 35:1, Psalm 43:1, Psalm 119:154, Micah 7:9), so the phrase alone cannot pick a source. Micah 7:9 is proposed because it is the only one of the five where God pleads the cause in the third person as a promise — “until he plead my cause” — and the only one that pairs the pleading with a judicial sentence executed on the adversary.
provenance.significance: Micah 7:9 is spoken by a sinner under sentence: “I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause.” Jacob 3 is addressed to a congregation two thirds of which is under exactly that sentence, and the promise of an advocate is offered to the pure-in-heart remainder. The Micah verse ends “he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness”, which is the light-and-darkness register Jacob returns to at 3:8-9.

links.note: “He will console you in your afflictions, and he will plead your cause, and send down justice upon those who seek your destruction.” Two of the three clauses answer to Micah 7:9's two: he pleads the cause, and he executes judgment. The third — consolation in affliction — has no KJV wording behind it; “console” is not a King James word at all, and its presence is a mark of the 1829 dictation rather than of a source. Recorded as an echo because the phrase it turns on is shared with four other verses; but note that 1 Samuel 24:15, one of those four, sits between the two verses that supply this chapter's frame at 3:5 and 3:14, which is a reason to keep it named in the composite rather than discard it.
links.whyNot: A five-verse phrase and no second point of contact. A reader who takes “plead your cause” as ordinary devotional English — which by 1829 it was — loses nothing by declining this row.
links.text: I will bear the indignation of the LORD, because I have sinned against him, until he plead my cause, and execute judgment for me: he will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold his righteousness.

pericopes.text: O all ye that are pure in heart, lift up your heads and receive the pleasing word of God, and feast upon his love; for ye may, if your minds are firm, forever.

provenance.other: “lift up your heads” occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Psalm 24:7, Psalm 24:9 and Luke 21:28. Two of the three are one psalm, and that psalm is also the KJV's principal text on purity of heart as the condition of approach — “He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart” (24:4).
provenance.alternative: Luke 21:28 is the better fit for the sense, since there the heads lifted are people's and the occasion is consolation — “then look up, and lift up your heads; for your redemption draweth nigh” — whereas Psalm 24's heads belong to the gates of the temple. The sequence favours the psalm and the meaning favours Luke; both are named.
provenance.significance: Read with Psalm 24 recovered, Jacob 3:1-2 reproduces the psalm's own order of business: who may ascend the hill of the LORD, he that has a pure heart, lift up your heads. Jacob has taken a liturgy of entrance and re-addressed it from the gates to the congregation, so that the pure in heart are themselves the doors through which the King of glory comes in.

links.note: “O all ye that are pure in heart, lift up your heads and receive the pleasing word of God.” Taken alone the phrase is unremarkable; taken in sequence with the KJV singleton “pure in heart” in the clause before it, it puts Jacob on the two halves of Psalm 24 in the psalm's own order. “Feast upon his love”, which closes the verse, has no KJV antecedent — the KJV never uses “feast” with a divine attribute as its object — and is the Book of Mormon's own idiom, recurring at 2 Nephi 9:51 and Jacob 3:2 alone in this book.
links.text: Lift up your heads, O ye gates; and be ye lift up, ye everlasting doors; and the King of glory shall come in.

pericopes.text: But, wo, wo, unto you that are not pure in heart; that are filthy this day before God; for except ye shall repent, the land is cursed for your sakes; and the Lamanites, which are not filthy like unto you, (nevertheless, they are cursed with a sore cursing) shall scourge you even unto destruction.

provenance.other: “cursed is the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Genesis 3:17, and it is the Bible's one statement that the land itself is cursed on account of somebody's conduct. “for your sakes” is common (fifteen KJV verses) but not in this construction: nowhere else does the KJV curse a territory for the sake of the people standing on it.
provenance.significance: The Fall's sentence is Adam's alone in Genesis; here it is conditional and reversible — “except ye shall repent, the land is cursed for your sakes”. A curse pronounced once on the ground for the first man's disobedience becomes, in Jacob's mouth, a standing offer withdrawable on repentance, and the land in question is a land of promise rather than a garden lost.

links.note: “For except ye shall repent, the land is cursed for your sakes.” The construction — land, cursed, on account of a person — exists once in the King James Bible and this is its shape. Note that Jacob turns the sentence's polarity: Genesis makes the curse the consequence of a sin already committed, Jacob makes it the consequence of a repentance not yet made.
links.text: And unto Adam he said, Because thou hast hearkened unto the voice of thy wife, and hast eaten of the tree, of which I commanded thee, saying, Thou shalt not eat of it: cursed is the ground for thy sake; in sorrow shalt thou eat of it all the days of thy life;

provenance.other: “cursed with a curse” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Malachi 3:9. The Book of Mormon reads “cursed with a sore cursing” — the same cognate-accusative Hebraism, with the noun changed and an adjective added. 1830 reads “the cursings which hath come upon their skins” at 3:5 where 1920 prints the singular “cursing”.
provenance.significance: Malachi 3:9-11 holds both halves of what Jacob 3:3 says in one breath: a nation “cursed with a curse”, and a land whose fruit God will or will not destroy “for your sakes” (3:11). If the collocation is borrowed rather than coincidental, Jacob has taken the vocabulary of a covenant lawsuit about withheld tithes and applied it to withheld chastity.

links.note: “The Lamanites, which are not filthy like unto you, (nevertheless, they are cursed with a sore cursing).” The cognate accusative is the KJV's at Malachi 3:9 and nowhere else, and the same page of Malachi supplies the “for your sakes” that governs the previous clause. Recorded as an echo, not an allusion, because the shared element is a construction rather than a string — “sore cursing” is not KJV English at all.
links.whyNot: A cognate accusative is a Hebraism available anywhere in the King James idiom, and the two contexts have nothing in common but the fact of a curse. The Malachi 3:11 “for your sakes” is a coincidence of a fifteen-verse phrase.
links.text: Ye are cursed with a curse: for ye have robbed me, even this whole nation.

pericopes.text: And the time speedily cometh, that except ye repent, they shall possess the land of your inheritance, and the Lord God will lead away the righteous out from among you.

Behold, the Lamanites your brethren, whom ye hate, because of their filthiness and the cursings which hath come upon their skins, are more righteous than you; for they have not forgotten the commandment of the Lord, which was given unto our fathers, that they should have, save it were one wife; and concubines they should have none; and there should not be whoredoms committed among them.

provenance.other: “are more righteous than” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ezekiel 16:52. The comparative in any person occurs in exactly four (Genesis 38:26, 1 Samuel 24:17, Ezekiel 16:52, Habakkuk 1:13), and of those four only Ezekiel has it in the plural and only Ezekiel is addressed to the guilty party about people she despises.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 16 is the KJV's longest sustained figure of sexual infidelity: Jerusalem as an adulterous wife, with Sodom and Samaria as her sisters, and the sting of 16:51-52 is that the sisters she has judged “are more righteous than thou” because her own abominations exceed theirs. Jacob 3:5 lands in the same place from the same premises. The sermon he is finishing is about wives and concubines and whoredoms; the people he tells his hearers to look at are their despised kin; and the verdict he delivers is the exact verdict Ezekiel delivers, in Ezekiel's words. Recovering the context supplies what Jacob does not say aloud: in Ezekiel the comparison is not a compliment to the sisters, it is a sentence on the one being addressed, and it ends “be thou confounded also, and bear thy shame”.

links.note: “The Lamanites your brethren, whom ye hate … are more righteous than you.” The verse turns on a KJV singleton, and the singleton comes from the one chapter of the King James Bible that argues at length that a people's sexual unfaithfulness makes its despised neighbours look righteous by comparison. Given that Jacob 2-3 is a single sermon on plural marriage and whoredom, the coincidence of wording and of subject is hard to put down to chance. The chapter has a second and independent claim on the phrase: see the 1 Samuel 24:17 row at this verse, where the David-and-Saul frame is argued.
links.text: Thou also, which hast judged thy sisters, bear thine own shame for thy sins that thou hast committed more abominable than they: they are more righteous than thou: yea, be thou confounded also, and bear thy shame, in that thou hast justified thy sisters.

provenance.other: “more righteous than” occurs in exactly four KJV verses; 1 Samuel 24:17 is the one in which the speaker concedes it to a man he has been hunting. The chapter's other two contacts are checkable in the same way: “end of speaking these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse (1 Samuel 24:16), and “plead my cause” in exactly five, of which 1 Samuel 24:15 is one.
provenance.significance: Three consecutive verses of 1 Samuel 24 stand at three structural points of Jacob 3 — 24:15 behind the promise that God “will plead your cause” in the opening sentence, 24:17 behind the chapter's central verdict, 24:16 behind its closing colophon. Recovered, the frame is the cave at En-gedi: David spares the king who is hunting him, calls on the LORD to plead his cause, and Saul answers, weeping, “Thou art more righteous than I.” Jacob is telling Nephites that the Lamanites hunting them hold David's position and they hold Saul's.

links.note: No single one of these three contacts would carry a link. Together they are the chapter's frame: the phrase that opens it, the verdict at its centre and the formula that closes it all come from 1 Samuel 24:15-17, in the biblical order, and the passage they come from is the Bible's set piece on a pursued man proving more righteous than the king pursuing him. That is the argument Jacob 3 is making about the Lamanites. Catalogued at moderate because each strand is individually thin and the case rests on their convergence; the reader who wants one strong verbal source for this verse should take the Ezekiel 16:52 row above.
links.whyNot: Convergence arguments are the easiest kind to manufacture: with 31,000 verses available, three loose contacts within one biblical chapter are not beyond coincidence, and “made an end of speaking” is a common enough KJV closing formula that its four-word extension may be accidental.
links.text: And he said to David, Thou art more righteous than I: for thou hast rewarded me good, whereas I have rewarded thee evil.

pericopes.text: And now this commandment they observe to keep; wherefore, because of this observance in keeping this commandment, the Lord God will not destroy them, but will be merciful unto them; and one day they shall become a blessed people.

Behold, their husbands love their wives, and their wives love their husbands, and their husbands and their wives love their children; and their unbelief and their hatred towards you, is because of the iniquity of their fathers; wherefore, how much better are you than they, in the sight of your Great Creator?

provenance.route: Titus 2:4 (+ Ephesians 5:25) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “love their husbands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “love their children” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse: Titus 2:4. The remaining clause, husbands loving wives, is the household code's other half at Ephesians 5:25 and Colossians 3:19.
provenance.significance: Jacob's evidence that the Lamanites are the more righteous people is a household in good order, and he describes it in the vocabulary of the Pauline household codes — the New Testament's own standard for a well-ordered Christian family. The metaleptic force is in what the codes are for: Titus 2 is instruction to a church on how to live so that “the word of God be not blasphemed”, and it is being satisfied, in Jacob's account, by the people his hearers despise. The unstated correspondence is that the Lamanites are keeping a rule the Nephites were given.

links.note: “Their husbands love their wives, and their wives love their husbands, and their husbands and their wives love their children.” Two of the three clauses reproduce the two KJV singletons of Titus 2:4 in Titus's order, and the third is Ephesians 5:25's imperative turned into a report. This is a Pauline household code assembled from two epistles and set inside a sermon against plural marriage — a monogamous ideal being described in the one register of the King James Bible that has vocabulary for it. Well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and catalogued as allusion, but the double singleton makes the identification of the source secure.
links.text: That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,

pericopes.text: O my brethren, I fear, that unless ye shall repent of your sins, that their skins will be whiter than yours, when ye shall be brought with them before the throne of God.

provenance.other: “before the throne of God” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 7:15 and Revelation 14:5, and 7:15 is the one that arrives with an explanation of how the people standing there came to be white: “made them white” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 7:14, and what is made white there is a robe washed in the blood of the Lamb.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's sharpest case of a borrowed phrase carrying its context against the borrower. Jacob imagines a joint appearance of Nephites and Lamanites in which the Lamanites' skins are the whiter, and the phrase he reaches for to describe the venue occurs twice in the King James Bible — once, at Revelation 7:15, four words after the only verse in scripture that says anyone was made white. There the whiteness is laundry, explicitly and at length: robes washed by people who came out of great tribulation. Whatever the verse intends about skin, the scriptural language it is standing in makes whiteness a thing done to a garment by the blood of the Lamb, and unavailable as a property of a body.

links.note: “Their skins will be whiter than yours, when ye shall be brought with them before the throne of God.” The catalogue's claim here is limited and worth stating exactly: the venue clause has a KJV source and the whiteness clause has none. “whiter than” occurs in exactly two KJV verses — Psalm 51:7's “whiter than snow”, of a sinner washed, and Lamentations 4:7's “whiter than milk”, of the Nazarites' polish — and neither is a comparison between two peoples' skins, which is a comparison the King James Bible does not make anywhere. The racial language of 3:5-9 (“filthiness”, “the darkness of their skins”, skins “whiter than yours”) is the Book of Mormon's own and is not being catalogued as scriptural vocabulary; where a phrase in this passage has no KJV source, the entry says so rather than proposing one. Compare the same handling at 1 Nephi 12:23.
links.text: Therefore are they before the throne of God, and serve him day and night in his temple: and he that sitteth on the throne shall dwell among them.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, a commandment I give unto you, which is the word of God, that ye revile no more against them, because of the darkness of their skins; neither shall ye revile against them because of their filthiness; but ye shall remember your own filthiness, and remember that their filthiness came because of their fathers.

provenance.other: “commandment I give unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 13:34, where the commandment given is that ye love one another. The Book of Mormon's clause is “a commandment I give unto you” for John's “A new commandment I give unto you”.
provenance.significance: The one commandment in the King James Bible introduced with these words is the commandment to love; the commandment Jacob introduces with them is a prohibition on reviling a hated people. Read with John recovered, the two are the same commandment stated from opposite ends — John says what to do, Jacob says what to stop — and Jacob's is the harder version, because it names the people it is about.

links.note: “Wherefore, a commandment I give unto you, which is the word of God, that ye revile no more against them, because of the darkness of their skins.” The introduction is a KJV singleton; the substance is not. “revile” is a nine-verse word in the KJV, but the chapter has been running on the Sermon on the Mount since its first sentence (see the Matthew 5:8 row at 3:1), and Matthew 5:11 — “Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you” — is three verses below the one Jacob started from, which is why it is named in the composite. Catalogued at moderate rather than high because a five-word formula introducing a commandment could be a preacher's cadence rather than a citation.
links.text: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, ye shall remember your children, how that ye have grieved their hearts, because of the example that ye have set before them; and also, remember that ye may, because of your filthiness, bring your children unto destruction, and their sins be heaped upon your heads at the last day.

O my brethren, hearken unto my word; arouse the faculties of your soul; shake yourselves, that ye may awake from the slumber of death; and loose yourselves from the pains of hell, that ye may not become Angels to the Devil, to be cast into that lake of fire and brimstone, which is the second death.

provenance.route: Isaiah 52:1-2 → KJV → Book of Mormon, possibly by way of 2 Nephi 8:24-25
provenance.other: “shake thyself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “loose thyself” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, Isaiah 52:2. Jacob has both verbs, reflexive, in Isaiah's order, with Isaiah 52:1's “Awake, awake” between them as “that ye may awake”. The object of the loosing is supplied from elsewhere: “pains of hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 116:3, “the pains of hell gat hold upon me”.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 52:1-2 is addressed to a captive city told to get up off the ground because the bands on her neck are already loose. Jacob applies it to men asleep in their own sin, and swaps Isaiah's bands of the neck for Psalm 116:3's pains of hell — so the captivity being shaken off is not Babylon but death. The two-source fusion is the finding: Isaiah supplies both reflexive verbs, the psalm supplies what is holding on.

links.note: “Shake yourselves, that ye may awake from the slumber of death; and loose yourselves from the pains of hell.” Three KJV singletons in one clause, two of them from a single verse. The mediation is genuinely undecidable and is recorded as such: 2 Nephi 8:24-25 has already transcribed Isaiah 52:1-2 into the Book of Mormon verbatim — “Shake thyself from the dust … loose thyself from the bands of thy neck” — so the proximate model may be the earlier Book of Mormon page rather than the KJV Isaiah, and because that transcription reproduces Isaiah exactly there is no divergence for tools/mediation-check.py to test. Where the diff cannot decide, the entry says so.
links.text: Shake thyself from the dust; arise, and sit down, O Jerusalem: loose thyself from the bands of thy neck, O captive daughter of Zion.

provenance.other: Three Revelation verses are in play and the Book of Mormon takes a half from two of them. “lake of fire and brimstone” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 20:10; Revelation 21:8 has instead “the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone”. The second half is decided by one word: “which is the second death” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 21:8, against Revelation 20:14's “This is the second death”, and the Book of Mormon reads “which”. “second death” at large occurs in four KJV verses, all in Revelation.
provenance.significance: The fusion produces a sentence in neither source: Revelation's lake of fire and brimstone (20:10, where the devil is cast) welded to Revelation's definition of the second death (21:8, where the fearful and the whoremongers are). Given that Jacob's sermon is against whoredom, the half he takes the relative clause from is the half whose list of the condemned includes whoremongers — and his hearers, warned three verses later against fornication, are on it.

links.note: “To be cast into that lake of fire and brimstone, which is the second death.” An eight-word run against Revelation 21:8 and a five-word run against 20:10, catalogued as a quotation on the strength of the reproduced clause rather than its length — it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his long quotations. The pronoun test is the useful part: “which is the second death” is 21:8's wording, not 20:14's “This is”, so the Book of Mormon has the verse that names whoremongers among those whose part it is.
links.text: But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.

provenance.other: “the devil and his angels” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:41. The Book of Mormon inverts the genitive: not the devil's angels but men who become “Angels to the Devil”, which is 2 Nephi 9:9's coinage (“Angels to a Devil”, so capitalized in 1830) reused here.
provenance.significance: Matthew 25:41 assigns the everlasting fire to the devil and his angels; the Book of Mormon's inversion makes the damned into the staff rather than the fuel. Read against Matthew, the sentence at the left hand — “Depart from me, ye cursed” — is the sentence Jacob is warning his hearers they will hear, and the chapter has already told them what being cursed looks like from the outside (3:3).

links.note: “That ye may not become Angels to the Devil, to be cast into that lake of fire and brimstone.” The phrase is the Book of Mormon's own, coined at 2 Nephi 9:9 and reused here, but its raw material is the KJV's single verse pairing the devil with angels belonging to him, and the destination clause that follows it is Revelation's. Recorded at moderate because the wording is inverted and the idea of the devil's angels is a commonplace of English preaching well outside the KJV.
links.text: Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels:

pericopes.text: And now I, Jacob, spake many more things unto the people of Nephi, warning them against fornication, and lasciviousness, and every kind of sin, telling them the awful consequences of them;

provenance.other: “fornication and lasciviousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:21. “lasciviousness” itself is a six-verse word (Mark 7:22, 2 Corinthians 12:21, Galatians 5:19, Ephesians 4:19, 1 Peter 4:3, Jude 1:4), and the pairing with fornication in that order is Paul's alone.
provenance.significance: Recovering 2 Corinthians 12:21 supplies Jacob's whole rhetorical situation, not just his two nouns. Paul is writing ahead of a visit, afraid that God will humble him among the Corinthians and that he will have to “bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented”. Jacob's summary of his sermon is a preacher warning a congregation about the same sins in the same fear, and his own “I fear, that unless ye shall repent” at 3:8 is the same sentence turned toward the hearers. The chapter takes from Paul both the vice list and the posture of the man reciting it.

links.note: “Warning them against fornication, and lasciviousness, and every kind of sin, telling them the awful consequences of them.” The pairing is a KJV singleton and it comes from the one verse in the epistles where an apostle says in advance that he expects his warning to fail. Galatians 5:19 is the nearer analogue for a vice list as such — “Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness” — but it separates the two words Jacob joins, which is why 2 Corinthians is preferred here.
links.text: And lest, when I come again, my God will humble me among you, and that I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented of the uncleanness and fornication and lasciviousness which they have committed.

pericopes.text: and a hundredth part of the proceedings of this people, which now began to be numerous, cannot be written upon these plates; but many of their proceedings are written upon the larger plates, and their wars, and their contentions, and the reigns of their kings.
These plates are called the plates of Jacob; and they were made by the hand of Nephi. And I make an end of speaking these words.

provenance.other: “end of speaking these words” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 24:16. “made an end of speaking” without the object is common — nine KJV verses — so the whole four-word extension is doing the identifying, and 1830's “I make an end of speaking these words” has all of it.
provenance.significance: The colophon is the third of the chapter's three contacts with 1 Samuel 24:15-17 (see the row at 3:5). What David finishes speaking in that verse is the speech that ends with Saul conceding “Thou art more righteous than I” and weeping — so the Book of Mormon's formula for ending a sermon is the KJV's formula for ending the speech whose verdict Jacob 3:5 has just delivered against his own people. The colophon and the sermon's thesis come from two adjacent verses of one chapter.

links.note: “These plates are called the plates of Jacob; and they were made by the hand of Nephi. And I make an end of speaking these words.” The colophon proper — the naming of the plates and their maker — has no KJV source and is the Book of Mormon's own scribal convention; only the closing formula is borrowed, and it is borrowed from a verse three verses away from the one behind 3:5. Catalogued at high on the singleton, at the recognized risk that a book which ends many chapters this way may simply have a house formula: cf. 1 Nephi 9:6 and Jacob 6:13 for the family of closings.
links.text: And it came to pass, when David had made an end of speaking these words unto Saul, that Saul said, Is this thy voice, my son David? And Saul lifted up his voice, and wept.

pericopes.text: Now behold, it came to pass, that I, Jacob, having ministered much unto my people, in word, (and I cannot write but a little of my words, because of the difficulty of engraving our words upon plates,) and we know that the things which we write upon plates, must remain;

but whatsoever things we write upon any thing save it be upon plates, must perish and vanish away; but we can write a few words upon plates, which will give our children, and also our beloved brethren, a small degree of knowledge concerning us, or concerning their fathers.

Now in this thing we do rejoice; and we labor diligently to engraven these words upon plates, hoping that our beloved brethren, and our children, will receive them with thankful hearts, and look upon them, that they may learn with joy, and not with sorrow, neither with contempt, concerning their first parents:

links.text: Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.

provenance.other: “with joy, and not with” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 13:17. The Book of Mormon completes the phrase with 'sorrow' where the KJV has 'grief', and then adds a third term, 'neither with contempt', which is its own.
provenance.significance: Hebrews 13:17 is addressed to a congregation about its leaders: obey them, because they watch for your souls as men who must give account, so that they may do it 'with joy, and not with grief'. Jacob has opened this chapter as exactly such a man — 'I, Jacob, having ministered much unto my people' — and the thing he wants received with joy is the account he is engraving. Recover the source and the borrowed clause turns out to be about a minister's reckoning for the people he served, which is what the plates are: Jacob's account, and the joy or grief with which his readers will take it. The letter's second-person burden ('that they may do it') has been transposed into the writer's hope for a reader four hundred years off.

links.note: 'Hoping that our beloved brethren, and our children, will receive them with thankful hearts, and look upon them, that they may learn with joy, and not with sorrow, neither with contempt.' Four words of Hebrews 13:17 in order, from the only KJV verse that has them, and the substitution of 'sorrow' for 'grief' is the kind of near-synonym exchange that marks a phrase carried in memory rather than copied. The two triads also correspond: Hebrews sets joy against grief and calls the alternative 'unprofitable for you'; Jacob sets joy against sorrow and against contempt, contempt being what makes an inheritance unprofitable to an heir.

pericopes.text: for, for this intent have we written these things, that they may know that we knew of Christ, and we had a hope of his glory, many hundred years before his coming; and not only we, ourselves, had a hope of his glory, but also all the Holy Prophets which were before us.

links.text: Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.

provenance.other: “the prophets which were before” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 5:12, where it ends 'before you'. Jacob 4:4 ends it 'before us'. The nearer synoptic parallel, Luke 6:23, reads 'so did their fathers unto the prophets' and does not have the phrase.
provenance.significance: The Beatitudes' last blessing is a blessing on a persecuted line: rejoice, because that is how they treated the prophets which were before you. Jacob takes the same five words and turns them from a consolation into a claim of company — the holy prophets before us also had a hope of his glory. The clause that in Matthew marks a succession of suffering marks in Jacob a succession of foreknowledge, and ten verses later, at 4:14, Jacob will supply the persecution Matthew's clause implies: the Jews 'killed the Prophets'.

links.note: 'And not only we, ourselves, had a hope of his glory, but also all the Holy Prophets which were before us.' The five-word run is a KJV singleton and the only change is the pronoun, which the sentence requires: Matthew's speaker addresses a persecuted 'you', Jacob's writes himself into the line as 'us'. The verse is well short of Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his quotations; it is catalogued here on rarity, not length. The 'hope of his glory', twice in this verse, is the KJV's 'the hope of glory' (Colossians 1:27, a singleton), which returns at 4:11 in fuller form and is adjudicated there.

pericopes.text: Behold, they believed in Christ, and worshiped the Father in his name; and also, we worship the Father in his name. And for this intent, we keep the law of Moses, it pointing our souls to him; and for this cause, it is sanctified unto us for righteousness, even as it was accounted unto Abraham in the wilderness, to be obedient unto the commands of God, in offering up his son Isaac, which was a similitude of God and his only begotten Son.

links.text: Even as Abraham believed God, and it was accounted to him for righteousness.

provenance.mt: Genesis 15:6 — 'And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.'
provenance.route: Genesis 15:6 → Galatians 3:6 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The KJV renders the Abraham formula four different ways. Genesis 15:6: 'he COUNTED it to him for righteousness'. Romans 4:3: 'it was COUNTED unto him for righteousness'. James 2:23: 'it was IMPUTED unto him for righteousness'. Galatians 3:6: 'it was ACCOUNTED to him for righteousness'. “accounted to him for righteousness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. Jacob 4:5 reads 'even as it was accounted unto Abraham'.
provenance.significance: A mediation case decided by one word, and the second in this chapter. Genesis 15:6 is quoted three times in the New Testament and the KJV translators gave it a different verb each time; the Book of Mormon has the verb of Galatians, not of Genesis, of Romans, or of James. Recover Galatians 3 and the argument around that verb is precisely Jacob's: whether the law is kept for its own sake or as a witness to Christ. Paul asks the Galatians whether they received the Spirit 'by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith' and then produces Abraham as the answer; Jacob says 'we keep the law of Moses, it pointing our souls to him', and produces Abraham as the same answer. The one word carries the whole chapter of Galatians behind it.
provenance.alternative: Hebrews 11:17-19, which also reads Abraham's obedience as faith, is the source of the second half of this verse (below) and would be available for the first half as well — but it does not contain the righteousness formula in any form.

links.note: 'It is sanctified unto us for righteousness, even as it was accounted unto Abraham … to be obedient unto the commands of God, in offering up his son Isaac.' `mediation-check.py` returns one decisive point here: 'was accounted' is Galatians 3:6's form and is in no other KJV verse. Note that the Book of Mormon has also moved the formula off Abraham's belief and onto his obedience — in all four biblical versions what is accounted for righteousness is that Abraham believed, whereas Jacob attaches it to the offering of Isaac, which is James 2:21-23's reading of the same verse fitted to Galatians' wording.

links.text: By faith Abraham, when he was tried, offered up Isaac: and he that had received the promises offered up his only begotten son,

provenance.other: “offered up his only begotten son” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:17, and it is the only place outside the Johannine writings where the KJV uses 'only begotten son' at all. Jacob 4:5 holds the offering of Isaac and 'his only begotten Son' in a single clause. Hardy's apparatus points Genesis 22:1-18 at this verse — the narrative itself, behind the Hebrews sentence that reports it. The reference was read as standing at Jacob 3:5 until the study edition's running heads were used to bound each page (2026-09-05); it belongs here, where Jacob names the offering of Isaac outright.
provenance.significance: In Hebrews the only begotten son IS Isaac; in Jacob the offering of Isaac is 'a similitude of God and his only begotten Son', so the title has slid from the type to the antitype while the sentence around it stays where Hebrews put it. That is the interesting move, and Frederick makes it: he observes that Hebrews 11:17 is the sole non-Johannine New Testament use of the title, that Jacob 4:4-5 uses it in the same setting of Abraham's sacrifice, and that the title 'has been switched from referring to Isaac in Hebrews 11:17 to referring to Jesus in Jacob 4:4-5'; on that basis, and because in his judgment Jacob echoes Paul more than John, he suggests the provenance of the verse is Hebrews rather than John. This catalogue reaches the same conclusion by a different route — the four-word run is a KJV singleton — and the agreement is worth something because the routes differ (CONVENTIONS §3a).
provenance.alternative: John 3:16 supplies 'his only begotten Son' with a giving Father and is the more familiar home of the phrase; Frederick's own note weighs and sets it aside for this verse.

links.note: 'In offering up his son Isaac, which was a similitude of God and his only begotten Son.' Hebrews 11:17 is the one KJV verse that puts the offering and the title together, and Jacob 4:5 is the one Book of Mormon verse that does. Frederick discusses Jacob 4:4-5 at length in a note on the Book of Mormon's use of 'Only Begotten Son' and argues for Hebrews over John here; he is not compiling an index of sources, so the observation is an argument about a title, not a citation entry, but it is a real attribution and it is on this verse. Note also 1 Nephi's route through Hebrews 11 in order (11:8, 11:9, 11:13, 11:29 across 1 Nephi 2-5): the chapter of Hebrews that supplied Lehi's departure supplies Jacob's Isaac.

links.text: But the hour cometh, and now is, when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and in truth: for the Father seeketh such to worship him.

provenance.other: “worship the Father in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 4:23, where the phrase completes as 'in spirit and in truth'. Jacob 4:5 completes it twice as 'in his name'. Frederick, discussing the clauses of D&C 20:29, notes that the phrase 'worship the Father in his name' is not found in John and locates it in only two places, 2 Nephi 25:16 and this verse.
provenance.significance: Whatever the route, the substitution is doctrinally the point of the verse: John's true worshippers are marked off by the manner of their worship, Jacob's by its name. He is arguing that pre-Christian Nephites are Christians, and the qualifier that does the work is the one he has changed.

links.whyNot: Only the four common words are shared, and each of them is common; the distinctive half of John's clause ('in spirit and in truth') is absent, and the distinctive half of Jacob's ('in his name') is absent from John. Frederick's observation that the full Book of Mormon phrase is not biblical cuts against a direct borrowing. The rarity count is real but four such words can co-occur by construction.
links.note: 'They believed in Christ, and worshiped the Father in his name; and also, we worship the Father in his name.' Recorded at moderate because the four-word sequence is a KJV singleton and because John 4 is the KJV's one sustained discussion of how the Father is to be worshipped, which is what this verse is doing; declined above moderate because the phrase that Jacob actually repeats twice is not a biblical phrase at all.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, we search the Prophets; and we have many revelations, and the spirit of prophecy; and having all these witnesses, we obtain a hope, and our faith becometh unshaken, insomuch that we truly can command in the name of Jesus, and the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea;

links.text: And I fell at his feet to worship him. And he said unto me, See thou do it not: I am thy fellowservant, and of thy brethren that have the testimony of Jesus: worship God: for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy.

provenance.other: “the spirit of prophecy” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 19:10: 'for the testimony of Jesus is the spirit of prophecy'.
provenance.significance: Jacob's list is 'we search the Prophets; and we have many revelations, and the spirit of prophecy; and having all these witnesses'. Revelation 19:10 is the verse that defines the borrowed term, and defines it as a testimony — 'the testimony of Jesus IS the spirit of prophecy' — which is exactly the use Jacob puts it to when he calls the three items witnesses. The definition travels with the phrase.

links.note: A KJV singleton, and the sense comes with it. The angel's refusal in Revelation 19:10 is also the scene 1 Nephi 17:55 borrowed for Nephi's brothers, so this chapter is drawing on a verse already in the corpus, but for the other half of it: 1 Nephi took the refusal, Jacob takes the definition.

links.text: And the Lord said, If ye had faith as a grain of mustard seed, ye might say unto this sycamine tree, Be thou plucked up by the root, and be thou planted in the sea; and it should obey you.

provenance.route: Luke 17:6 (the tree) + Matthew 21:21 / Mark 11:23 (the mountain) + Mark 4:41 / Matthew 8:27 (the sea) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “obey you” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, of which only Luke 17:6 has an inanimate thing obeying — the sycamine tree, a KJV hapax. “and the sea obey” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Mark 4:41 and Matthew 8:27, both of the same stilling. The mountain moved by faith is Matthew 17:20, Matthew 21:21 and Mark 11:23.
provenance.significance: Jacob names three obedient things in one breath — 'the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea' — and the KJV has exactly one faith-saying for each, in the same order they are conventionally taught: the tree that should obey you (Luke 17:6), the mountain removed and cast into the sea (Matthew 21:21), the wind and the sea that obey him (Mark 4:41). The list is not a general claim about nature; it is a catalogue of the Gospels' three demonstrations, and the verb Jacob uses for all three is the verb Luke uses for the first and Mark for the third.

links.note: 'Insomuch that we truly can command in the name of Jesus, and the very trees obey us, or the mountains, or the waves of the sea.' No long run, which is why the machine streams found only the commonplace 'in the name of Jesus' here; the case is that three separate KJV faith-sayings are compressed into one clause with their distinctive nouns intact, and that Jacob's 'obey' is the Gospels' word in two of the three. The transposition is that in the KJV the sea obeys HIM and the tree would obey YOU if you had faith; Jacob claims both for the ministers.

pericopes.text: nevertheless, the Lord God sheweth us our weakness, that we may know that it is by his grace, and his great condescentions unto the children of men, that we have power to do these things.

Behold, great and marvellous are the works of the Lord.— How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of Him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.— And no man knoweth of his ways, save it be revealed unto him; wherefore, brethren, despise not the revelations of God.

links.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: “great and marvellous” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Revelation 15:1 and 15:3, and only 15:3 continues 'are thy works'. The 1830 edition spells the word 'marvellous', which is the KJV's spelling; 1920 modernized it to 'marvelous' and the borrowing is fainter in the modern text than in the first edition (CONVENTIONS §8).
provenance.significance: This is the same verse 1 Nephi 1:14 used for Lehi's praise, and the argument made there applies again: Revelation 15:3 labels the words it lends as 'the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb'. Across the book boundary the borrowing changes hands — Lehi sang it, Jacob preaches from it — and it changes person with them, 'thy works' becoming 'the works of the Lord'. What Jacob then does with it is new: Revelation's next clause is 'just and true are thy WAYS', and Jacob's next two clauses are about God's ways being unsearchable and no man knowing them. He has taken the couplet and turned its second half into the problem the rest of the paragraph solves.

links.note: 'Behold, great and marvellous are the works of the Lord.' Four words in order from one of the two KJV verses that has them, with 'thy works' converted to third person for a sermon rather than a hymn. Adjudicated afresh here rather than by cross-reference because this is a new book and a new voice (ADJUDICATING §4); the first adjudication is at 1 Nephi 1:14, where the same verse is borrowed in the second person as praise.

links.text: O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out!

provenance.other: “how unsearchable” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:33, and “the depth of the riches” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one; “past finding out” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:33 and Job 9:10. Jacob 4:8 has the depth, the 'how unsearchable', and the finding out, in Romans's order.
provenance.significance: This is the doorway into the chapter's controlling source. Romans 11:33 is the doxology that closes Paul's argument about Israel's blindness and stumbling, and Jacob 4:8 borrows it six verses before he starts making that argument himself: blindness (4:14), stumbling (4:14-15), the stone (4:15-17), and 'I will unfold this mystery' (4:18), which is Romans 11:25's 'this mystery' about the same blindness. Paul reaches the doxology at the end of Romans 11 and Jacob puts it at the beginning of his own version, so that the whole discourse on the Jews is framed as an instance of what the doxology says: his ways are past finding out. Recovering Romans 11 is what makes 4:8's apparently free-standing piety a thesis statement.

links.note: 'How unsearchable are the depths of the mysteries of Him; and it is impossible that man should find out all his ways.' Romans 11:33 reads 'O the depth of the riches … how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out'. Three of its distinctive elements — depth, 'how unsearchable', and the impossibility of finding out his ways — arrive in order, with 'judgments' exchanged for 'mysteries'. The exchange is not neutral: mystery is Romans 11:25's own word for what Paul is about to disclose, and Jacob will use it at 4:18.

pericopes.text: For behold, by the power of his word, man came upon the face of the earth; which earth was created by the power of his word. Wherefore, if God, being able to speak, and the world was; and to speak, and man was created, O then, why not able to command the earth, or the workmanship of his hands upon the face of it, according to his will and pleasure.

links.text: Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.

provenance.route: Hebrews 11:3 + Psalm 33:9 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the worlds were framed” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:3; “he spake, and it was” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 33:9 ('For he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast'). Jacob 4:9 reads 'if God, being able to speak, and the world was; and to speak, and man was created'.
provenance.significance: The double construction — speak, and the thing is — is Psalm 33:9's, which the KJV gives as a couplet of speaking and commanding; Jacob keeps the couplet and turns its second half into his argument, 'why not able to COMMAND the earth'. Hebrews 11:3 supplies the doctrine that the agent of creation is the word, which is the premise Jacob needs; and it is the third borrowing from Hebrews 11 in five verses, after 11:17 at 4:5.

links.note: 'By the power of his word, man came upon the face of the earth; which earth was created by the power of his word.' No long run: the case is that two KJV singletons stand behind the two halves of the sentence, and that Jacob's inference (God spoke the world into being, therefore he can command it) is Psalm 33:9's own move from speaking to commanding. Recorded at moderate because creation-by-word is common enough in the KJV that no single verse is compelled.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, brethren, seek not to counsel the Lord, but to take counsel from his hand. For behold, ye yourselves know, that he counseleth in wisdom, and in justice, and in great mercy, over all his works;

links.text: The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

provenance.other: “over all his works” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 145:9: 'The LORD is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.'
provenance.significance: 1 Nephi opened on this verse — 'the tender mercies of the Lord is over all them whom he hath chosen' — and Jacob closes a paragraph on it, and both keep the mercy: Nephi kept the tender mercies and dropped the works, Jacob keeps the works and folds the mercy into a triad, 'in wisdom, and in justice, and in great mercy, over all his works'. The Psalm's claim is that God's mercy has the same extent as his making; Jacob's context is a warning not to counsel the Lord, so the borrowed clause functions as the reason the counsel is unnecessary. Half a verse of Psalm 145 has now framed both ends of the small plates.

links.note: A KJV singleton, and the second appearance of Psalm 145:9 in the corpus after 1 Nephi 1:20. Written as a fresh link rather than a cross-reference because Jacob is a different hand and a reader of Jacob shown nothing here would be told there is no borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4); the argument for the source itself was made at 1 Nephi 1:20. Note that the n-gram stream missed the verse there, where the agreement was split across a clause boundary, and found it here, where it is contiguous — the same source, visible or invisible depending on how the borrower phrased it.

pericopes.text: wherefore, beloved brethren, be reconciled unto him, through the atonement of Christ, his only begotten Son, that ye may obtain a resurrection, according to the power of the resurrection which is in Christ, and be presented as the first fruits of Christ, unto God, having faith, and obtained a good hope of glory in him, before he manifesteth himself in the flesh.

links.text: Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.

provenance.route: 2 Corinthians 5:20 + 1 Corinthians 15:20-23 + Philippians 3:10 + Colossians 1:27 + 1 Timothy 3:16 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Five KJV rarities in one sentence: “be ye reconciled” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 5:20; “the power of the resurrection” occurs in no KJV verse, against Philippians 3:10's 'the power of his resurrection'; “the hope of glory” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Colossians 1:27; “good hope” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 2:16; “manifest in the flesh” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Timothy 3:16. 'Firstfruits' of Christ is 1 Corinthians 15:20-23, the KJV's one use of the term for the risen Christ.
provenance.significance: The verse is a Pauline cento, and the parts have not been chosen at random: reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5), resurrection and firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15), the power of the resurrection (Philippians 3), the hope of glory (Colossians 1), manifestation in the flesh (1 Timothy 3). What Jacob adds is the tense. Paul's firstfruits is Christ already risen; Jacob's readers are to be 'presented as the first fruits of Christ' before he 'manifesteth himself in the flesh', so the whole Pauline vocabulary of accomplished redemption is being used prospectively, by men who date themselves 'many hundred years before his coming' (4:4). That is the chapter's governing conceit, and this verse is where it is densest.

links.note: 'Be reconciled unto him, through the atonement of Christ, his only begotten Son, that ye may obtain a resurrection, according to the power of the resurrection which is in Christ, and be presented as the first fruits of Christ, unto God, having faith, and obtained a good hope of glory in him, before he manifesteth himself in the flesh.' Every clause has a KJV home and four of the five phrases are singletons; no single Pauline verse accounts for more than one clause, so 2 Corinthians 5:20 is listed as the source for the governing imperative and the rest as composite. 1830 reads 'first fruits' as two words, which is the KJV's spelling at 1 Corinthians 15:20 ('firstfruits') only in part — the KJV has both forms, and 1920 hyphenated Jacob's. Frederick quotes this verse in full when tracing the Book of Mormon's use of 'Only Begotten Son', and reads it as the most explicit of those uses; he does not propose a source for it.

pericopes.text: And now, beloved, marvel not that I tell you these things; for why not speak of the atonement of Christ, and attain to a perfect knowledge of him, as to attain to the knowledge of a resurrection and the world to come?

links.text: Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.

provenance.other: “marvel not that I” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 3:7: 'Marvel not that I said unto thee, Ye must be born again.' Jacob 4:12 reads 'marvel not that I tell you these things'. The nearest competitors are 1 John 3:13 ('Marvel not, my brethren, if the world hate you') and John 5:28 ('Marvel not at this'), neither of which has the construction.
provenance.significance: Jesus says it to Nicodemus, who has just objected that a man cannot be born a second time; the marvelling being forbidden is a teacher's incredulity at a doctrine that reorders time. Jacob's next clause — 'for why not speak of the atonement of Christ, and attain to a perfect knowledge of him' — asks his readers to accept a knowledge of Christ centuries before Christ, which is the same species of temporal impossibility. The borrowed opening carries its original occasion: an authority told not to be surprised by a chronology he cannot fit.

links.note: A KJV singleton and one of the chapter's cleanest borrowings. Note that the verse sits eight verses before John 3:16, whose 'only begotten Son' Jacob has already used twice (4:5, 4:11) — the chapter's contacts with John 3 are with the beginning and the end of one conversation.

pericopes.text: Behold, my brethren, he that prophesieth, let him prophesy to the understanding of men; for the spirit speaketh the truth, and lieth not. Wherefore, it speaketh of things as they really are, and of things as they really will be; wherefore, these things are manifested unto us plainly, for the salvation of our souls. But behold, we are not witnesses alone in these things; for God also spake them unto Prophets of old.

But behold, the Jews were a stiffnecked people; and they despised the words of plainness, and killed the Prophets, and sought for things that they could not understand. Wherefore, because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall: for God hath taken away his plainness from them, and delivered unto them many things which they cannot understand, because they desired it. And because they desired it, God hath done it, that they may stumble.

links.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

provenance.other: “this mystery” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:25 and Colossians 1:27, both of which stand behind this chapter (Colossians 1:27 at 4:11). Romans 11:25 is the KJV's only verse joining a mystery, blindness and Israel; Romans 11:11 supplies 'have they stumbled that they should fall', which is the exact pairing Jacob makes here — 'they must needs fall' because they 'stumble'.
provenance.significance: Jacob's causal chain is Paul's, in Paul's order and with Paul's terms: the Jews are blind, the blindness is judicial (God 'hath taken away his plainness from them', against Romans 11:8's 'God hath given them the spirit of slumber'), it makes them stumble, and the stumbling brings a fall. Paul's word for the whole business is mystery, and Jacob will say 'I will unfold this mystery' four verses later. Where the two differ is the cause: Paul assigns Israel's blindness to God's sovereign arrangement for the Gentiles, and Jacob assigns it to what the Jews wanted — 'because they desired it. And because they desired it, God hath done it' — which is Romans 1:24-28's mechanism imported into Romans 11's argument.

links.note: 'Because of their blindness, which blindness came by looking beyond the mark, they must needs fall … God hath done it, that they may stumble.' No long verbal run, and the machine streams proposed nothing at all for this verse; the case is structural — blindness, judicial hardening, stumbling, falling, and a mystery to be disclosed, which is the sequence of Romans 11:7-25 and occurs nowhere else in the KJV as a sequence. 'Looking beyond the mark' is Jacob's own figure and is in no KJV verse; it is the one piece of the chain that is not Paul's.

links.text: Wherefore ye be witnesses unto yourselves, that ye are the children of them which killed the prophets.

provenance.route: Matthew 23:31 (or 1 Thessalonians 2:15) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “killed the prophets” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 23:31 ('the children of them which killed the prophets'); 1 Thessalonians 2:15 has 'killed the Lord Jesus, and their own prophets'; Matthew 23:37 has 'thou that killest the prophets'. Jacob 4:14 reads 'and killed the Prophets'.
provenance.significance: Both candidates are indictments of a people for the same act, and both are in contexts Jacob is already using: Matthew 23 is the woes on scribes who 'shut up the kingdom of heaven against men', which is Jacob's charge that they 'despised the words of plainness'; 1 Thessalonians 2:15-16 runs on into wrath come upon them 'to the uttermost', which is Jacob's 'they must needs fall'.

links.note: A three-word KJV singleton in a verse that is otherwise carried by Romans 11, and one of the two verses that put the whole indictment in one clause. Left at moderate because the phrase is short and because the two candidates cannot be separated on wording — Matthew has the exact form, Paul has the sentiment and the consequence.

pericopes.text: And now I, Jacob, am led on by the spirit unto prophesying: for I perceive by the workings of the spirit which is in me, that by the stumbling of the Jews, they will reject the stone upon which they might build, and have safe foundation.

links.text: Wherefore? Because they sought it not by faith, but as it were by the works of the law. For they stumbled at that stumblingstone;

provenance.route: Romans 9:32-33 (with Isaiah 8:14) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “stumblingstone” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 9:32 and 9:33; “a stone of stumbling” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 8:14 and 1 Peter 2:8. Romans 9:32-33 is the KJV's one place where Israel's stumbling and the stone are a single figure: 'they stumbled at that stumblingstone; as it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence.'
provenance.significance: This is the hinge of the chapter and the reason its two halves belong together. Jacob has just said the Jews stumble (4:14); he now says that 'by the stumbling of the Jews, they will reject the stone upon which they might build'. Only in Romans 9:32-33 does the KJV make the thing stumbled over and the thing rejected the same stone, and it does so by fusing Isaiah 8:14's stone of stumbling with Isaiah 28:16's tried and precious foundation — which is precisely the fusion Jacob then performs across 4:15-17, running from the stumbling to the sure foundation (Isaiah 28:16) to the head of the corner (Psalm 118:22). Jacob is not quoting Romans; he is reproducing Romans's composite stone.

links.note: 'By the stumbling of the Jews, they will reject the stone upon which they might build, and have safe foundation.' The verbal contact is thin — stumbling, stone, reject — and the argument is that the combination is not. In the KJV the stone is either a stumblingblock (Isaiah 8:14) or a foundation (Isaiah 28:16) or a rejected head of the corner (Psalm 118:22); it is Romans 9 and 1 Peter 2 that weld the three into one figure, and Jacob has the welded figure. Note that Jacob adds a possibility the New Testament passages do not — the stone is one they MIGHT build on, and 4:17 asks whether they can yet.

pericopes.text: But behold, according to the Scriptures, this stone shall become the great, and the last, and the only sure foundation, upon which the Jews can build.

links.text: Therefore thus saith the Lord GOD, Behold, I lay in Zion for a foundation a stone, a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation: he that believeth shall not make haste.

provenance.mt: Isaiah 28:16 — 'a tried stone, a precious corner stone, a sure foundation'.
provenance.other: “sure foundation” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 28:16. The New Testament quotations of Isaiah 28:16 — Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:6 — both drop the phrase: Romans has 'a stumblingstone and rock of offence' and 1 Peter 'a chief corner stone, elect, precious'. So the one distinctive phrase Jacob takes is the one the New Testament does not carry.
provenance.significance: A mediation result in the negative, and it matters because 4:17 will go the other way. Isaiah 28:16 is quoted twice in the New Testament and neither quotation preserves 'sure foundation'; Jacob has it, twice ('the only sure foundation', 4:16; 'the sure foundation', 4:17). So the stone material in this chapter is not taken wholesale from one testament: the foundation comes from the Hebrew prophet in the KJV's Old Testament wording, and the corner, one verse later, comes from the Gospels' wording of the Psalm. Two verses, two directions.

links.note: 'This stone shall become the great, and the last, and the only sure foundation, upon which the Jews can build.' 'Sure foundation' is a KJV singleton and Jacob has flagged the borrowing himself — 'according to the Scriptures'. Hardy's appendix gives Isaiah 28:16 here. Note that 'the great, and the last' is not Isaiah's; the KJV's 'first and the last' formula belongs to Isaiah 44:6 and Revelation 1:11, and Jacob has replaced 'first' with 'great', which is the only word in the sentence that is his.

pericopes.text: And now, my beloved, how is it possible that these, after having rejected the sure foundation, can ever build upon it, that it may become the head of their corner?

links.text: The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.

provenance.mt: Psalm 118:22 — 'The stone which the builders refused is become the head stone of the corner.'
provenance.route: Psalm 118:22 → Matthew 21:42 / Mark 12:10 / Luke 20:17 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: Psalm 118:22 is quoted five times in the KJV New Testament and the KJV wording differs at two points. (1) The verb: the Psalm has 'refused'; Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17 have 'rejected'; Acts 4:11 has 'set at nought of you builders'; 1 Peter 2:7 has 'disallowed'. (2) The noun: the Psalm has 'the head STONE of the corner'; all five New Testament quotations have 'the head of the corner', with no 'stone'. Jacob 4:15 reads 'they will reject the stone', 4:17 'after having rejected the sure foundation … that it may become the head of their corner'. “the head of their corner” occurs in no KJV verse; “the builders refused” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; “the builders rejected” occurs in exactly three KJV verses, all Synoptic.
provenance.significance: The chapter's mediation test, and the book of Jacob's first. The Book of Mormon has the New Testament's form at both points where the KJV's Old Testament and New Testament differ — 'rejected', not 'refused'; 'the head of the corner', not 'the head stone of the corner'. And it has the Synoptic form specifically: Acts 4:11 rewords the verb entirely ('set at nought of you builders') and 1 Peter 2:7 gives 'disallowed', so of the five New Testament witnesses only Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10 and Luke 20:17 supply 'rejected'. The result confirms the pattern 1 Nephi established at 2:22, 6:4, 10:8, 15:18 and 22:20, where the borrowed Old Testament text arrives in its New Testament clothes; the recorded counter-examples are 1 Nephi 13:37 and 19:17, both Isaiah 52. Metalepsis does the rest: in all three Synoptics the verse is the punchline of the parable of the wicked husbandmen, spoken by Jesus to the chief priests about themselves, and Matthew's next words are 'the kingdom of God shall be taken from you'. Jacob asks 'how is it possible that these, after having rejected the sure foundation, can ever build upon it' — which is the parable's question, put by a man who says he is prophesying four hundred years before the parable is told.
provenance.alternative: Acts 4:11 and 1 Peter 2:7 are the two New Testament quotations that reword the verb; neither can be the source, since Jacob has 'reject' at 4:15 and 4:17.

links.note: 'That it may become the head of their corner.' `mediation-check.py` reports no decisive divergence for this verse, and that verdict is wrong in an instructive way: the tool cannot score an ABSENCE, so it could not see that Jacob lacks the Psalm's 'stone' in 'the head STONE of the corner' exactly as the New Testament quotations lack it. Read by eye, the verse is decided twice over — once by the missing 'stone' and once by 'rejected' against the Psalm's 'refused' — and both times on the New Testament side, and within the New Testament on the Synoptic side. This is the same class of trap ADJUDICATING §4 records for pronouns: the check ignores what is not there. Hardy's appendix gives all five references at this verse without choosing among them; the choice is the finding.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.17 (Psalm 118:22, Matthew 21:42, Mark 12:10, Luke 20:17, Acts 4:11)

pericopes.text: Behold, my beloved brethren, I will unfold this mystery, unto you; if I do not, by any means, get shaken from my firmness in the spirit, and stumble because of my over anxiety for you.

links.text: For I would not, brethren, that ye should be ignorant of this mystery, lest ye should be wise in your own conceits; that blindness in part is happened to Israel, until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.

provenance.other: “this mystery” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 11:25 and Colossians 1:27. Romans 11:25's mystery is Israel's partial blindness; Colossians 1:27's is 'Christ in you, the hope of glory', which this chapter has already used at 4:11.
provenance.significance: Jacob announces the mystery he is about to unfold and then unfolds it in Jacob 5, the allegory of the olive tree — which is Romans 11:17-24's figure, the natural branches broken off and the wild grafted in. So the chapter's last verse and the next chapter's whole content sit inside the passage that has been supplying its vocabulary since 4:8: Romans 11's doxology opened the discourse, Romans 11's blindness and stumbling carried 4:14, and Romans 11's mystery introduces the olive tree. Paul's own order is doxology last; Jacob has inverted it and put the doxology first.

links.whyNot: Two words, both ordinary, and 'unfold this mystery' is not a KJV construction — the KJV's verbs for a mystery are 'make known' and 'be ignorant of'. The link rests almost entirely on the surrounding Romans 11 material at 4:8 and 4:14 and on what Jacob 5 turns out to be; taken alone the verse would not carry it.
links.note: 'I will unfold this mystery, unto you.' Recorded as the closing bracket on the chapter's Romans 11 frame rather than as an independent borrowing. The confirmation is in the next chapter: Hardy's appendix gives Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9 and Romans 11:17-24 for the allegory Jacob is here promising, and Romans 11:25 is the verse that stands between Paul's olive tree and his doxology, exactly where Jacob's announcement stands between his own doxology (4:8) and his olive tree.

pericopes.text: Behold, my brethren, do ye not remember to have read the words of the Prophet Zenos, which spake unto the House of Israel, saying:
Hearken O ye House of Israel, and hear the words of me, a Prophet of the Lord:
for behold, thus saith the Lord, I will liken thee, O House of Israel, like unto a tame olive tree, which a man took and nourished in his vineyard; and it grew, and waxed old, and began to decay.

links.text: The LORD called thy name, A green olive tree, fair, and of goodly fruit: with the noise of a great tumult he hath kindled fire upon it, and the branches of it are broken.

provenance.other: “green olive tree” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 52:8 and Jeremiah 11:16. Only Jeremiah 11:16 makes the olive tree a name for the covenant people, and only there are its branches broken and fire kindled upon it.
provenance.significance: Romans 11 supplies the mechanics of Jacob 5 — the wild stock, the grafting, the natural branches — but not the identification of Israel with an olive tree that the Lord himself planted and named. That is Jeremiah's, and Jeremiah's olive tree ends exactly where the middle of this allegory ends: branches broken, fire kindled on it. Jeremiah 11 is a covenant-lawsuit chapter, which is the genre Jacob 5 is working in from 5:41 onward.

links.note: 'I will liken thee, O House of Israel, like unto a tame olive tree, which a man took and nourished in his vineyard.' The KJV has only two horticultural systems for this figure and Jacob 5 uses both: an olive tree standing for Israel (Jeremiah 11:16, Hosea 14:6) and a vineyard standing for Israel (Isaiah 5:7). Zenos's first sentence fuses them by planting the olive tree inside the vineyard, which no biblical verse does. Held at moderate because no clause is reproduced; the case is the identification plus the fate of the branches.

links.text: In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.

provenance.other: “decayeth” occurs in exactly three KJV verses and “waxeth old” in exactly two; Hebrews 8:13 is the only verse in the Bible that holds both, and it is the only place the KJV pairs decay with growing old.
provenance.significance: Recover the context and the borrowing does theological work the allegory never states. What 'decayeth and waxeth old' in Hebrews 8:13 is the first covenant, made old by the announcement of a new one and 'ready to vanish away' — and what waxes old and begins to decay in Jacob 5:3 is the house of Israel under exactly that covenant. The whole apparatus of the allegory (pruning, grafting, a last nourishing) is then an answer to Hebrews' verdict: the old tree is not allowed to vanish away, it is dug about.

links.note: 'And it grew, and waxed old, and began to decay.' Two uncommon KJV words in six, and the one verse that joins them is Hebrews 8:13. The 1830 reading is 'waxed old, and began to decay', preserving the KJV's verb pair intact. Held at moderate rather than high because the collocation is natural English as well as scriptural English, and a writer describing an old tree might reach it unaided; the rarity count is what makes it worth recording.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the master of the vineyard went forth, and he saw that his olive tree began to decay; and he sayeth, I will prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it, that perhaps it may shoot forth young and tender branches, and it perish not.

links.text: And he answering said unto him, Lord, let it alone this year also, till I shall dig about it, and dung it:

provenance.other: “dig about it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “dung it” occurs in exactly one KJV verse — both Luke 13:8. The verb 'to dig about' a tree exists nowhere else in the Authorized Version, and 'dung' as a transitive verb exists nowhere else either.
provenance.significance: Two of this chapter's most repeated actions are drawn from a single KJV verse in which a servant asks for one more season before a fruitless tree is cut down. That request is also the shape of Jacob 5:27 and 5:50 — 'nourish it a little longer', 'Spare it a little longer' — so the allegory has taken not only the vinedresser's vocabulary but his rhetorical role. What Luke gives in four verses, Zenos runs for seventy-seven.

links.note: 'I will prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it.' The pairing recurs across the chapter and reaches its full form at 5:47 ('I have nourished it, and I have digged it, and I have pruned it, and I have dunged it') and 5:76 ('pruned it, and dug about it, and dunged it'), which is Luke 13:8's two verbs together. Neither word is available anywhere else in the KJV, so the phrasing of the Lord of the vineyard's programme of care is Luke's, in a chapter whose subject Luke's parable shares.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24), the cross-reference standing at the head of the allegory

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that he pruned it, and digged about it, and nourished it, according to his word.
And it came to pass that after many days, it began to put forth somewhat a little, young and tender branches; but behold, the main top thereof began to perish.

And it came to pass that the master of the vineyard saw it, and he sayeth unto his servant, It grieveth me that I should lose this tree; wherefore, go and pluck the branches from a wild olive tree, and bring them hither unto me; and we will pluck off those main branches which are beginning to wither away, and we will cast them into the fire, that they may be burned.

links.text: And if some of the branches be broken off, and thou, being a wild olive tree, wert graffed in among them, and with them partakest of the root and fatness of the olive tree;

provenance.other: “wild olive tree” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:17, and “natural branches” in exactly two, Romans 11:21 and 11:24.
