Outside Romans 11 the Bible contains no grafting of any kind. But note the orthography: the KJV spells the verb 'graff' at all four places in Romans 11, and Jacob 5 spells it 'graft' throughout, in 1830 as in the current text.
provenance.significance: This is the verse where the claim already entered at 1 Nephi 10:12 and 15:13 is tested at length. There the catalogue argued that Romans 11 is the Book of Mormon's master allegory and named Jacob 5 in advance as the allegory expanded into a parable; here every one of Paul's terms is present and moving — branches broken off, a wild olive tree plucked and grafted in their stead, natural branches preserved elsewhere, and at 5:52-68 the natural branches grafted back into their own tree. Paul's whole point in Romans 11 is that the last of those is coming; Jacob 5 is that clause dramatised. The one thing the Book of Mormon adds to Paul is the nethermost part of the vineyard — the branches hidden elsewhere — which is what the allegory needs in order to be about a New World remnant as well as about Israel.

links.note: 'Go and pluck the branches from a wild olive tree, and bring them hither unto me; and we will pluck off those main branches which are beginning to wither away.' Romans 11:17 in reverse order, with Romans 11:19's 'the branches were broken off, that I might be graffed in' behind it. The chapter never quotes Paul continuously, which is why this is an allusion and not a quotation; what it does instead is run his figure forward for seventy-seven verses. The 'graff'/'graft' spelling difference is worth registering as a limit on how mechanical the borrowing is: the concept and the vocabulary are the KJV's, the orthography is the writer's own.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

pericopes.text: And behold, saith the Lord of the vineyard, I take away many of these young and tender branches, and I will graft them whithersoever I will; and it mattereth not that if it so be, that the root of this tree will perish, I may preserve the fruit thereof unto myself; wherefore, I will take these young and tender branches, and I will graft them whithersoever I will.

links.text: So when even was come, the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward, Call the labourers, and give them their hire, beginning from the last unto the first.

provenance.other: “lord of the vineyard” occurs in exactly four KJV verses: Matthew 20:8, Mark 12:9, Luke 20:13 and Luke 20:15. All four are inside a parable — the labourers hired at the eleventh hour, and the husbandmen who kill the son. The Book of Mormon's own longest run against any of them stands at 5:71, where the 1830 text reads 'the Lord of the vineyard saith unto them' against Matthew 20:8's 'the lord of the vineyard saith unto his steward' — seven consecutive words.
provenance.significance: The title by which God is named some fifty times in this chapter exists in the King James Bible only as the name of a character in two parables, and in both of them the vineyard is taken out of the hands of those who hold it. Recovering that context makes the allegory's ending predictable before it arrives: Matthew 20:8's lord pays 'beginning from the last unto the first', and Jacob 5:63 will graft 'beginning at the last, that they may be first'. The Book of Mormon has not merely borrowed a title; it has borrowed the parable the title belongs to and finished it differently.

links.note: 'And behold, saith the Lord of the vineyard, I take away many of these young and tender branches.' First appearance of the chapter's governing title. The 1830 text is also evidence here: it spells the verb 'sayeth' twenty-six times in this chapter and 'saith' only six, and the KJV form clusters exactly where the KJV phrase does — 5:8, 5:31 and 5:71, all three of them 'the Lord of the vineyard saith'. Where the borrowed formula is in play the borrowed spelling comes with it.

pericopes.text: Take thou the branches of the wild olive tree, and graft them in, in the stead thereof; and these which I have plucked off, I will cast into the fire, and burn them, that they may not cumber the ground of my vineyard.

links.text: Then said he unto the dresser of his vineyard, Behold, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree, and find none: cut it down; why cumbereth it the ground?

provenance.other: “why cumbereth it the ground” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The verb 'cumber' occurs in only one other place in the Authorized Version, Luke 10:40, where Martha is 'cumbered about much serving'. There is no other biblical warrant for the idea of a plant cumbering ground.
provenance.significance: Luke 13:6-9 is the one KJV parable in which an owner wants a fruitless tree destroyed, a servant asks for a stay, and the tree is given one more season of digging and dunging. Jacob 5 keeps every element and multiplies it: the complaint at 5:9 and 5:49, the servant's stay at 5:27 and 5:50, the digging and dunging at 5:47 and 5:76. The whole seventy-seven-verse shape of the allegory — a proprietor repeatedly talked out of felling — is Luke 13:6-9 held open.

links.note: 'These which I have plucked off, I will cast into the fire, and burn them, that they may not cumber the ground of my vineyard.' Cumbering the ground is Luke's idea and Luke's word, and the Book of Mormon uses it three times (5:9, 5:49, 5:66), always of what must be cleared out of the vineyard. Note that the KJV asks it as a question and the Book of Mormon states it as a purpose, which is the usual direction of this chapter's borrowing: Luke's parable poses the problem, Zenos's allegory acts on it.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the servant of the Lord of the vineyard, done according to the word of the Lord of the vineyard, and grafted in the branches of the wild olive tree.

And the Lord of the vineyard caused that it should be digged about, and pruned, and nourished, saying unto his servant, It grieveth me that I should lose this tree; wherefore, that perhaps I might preserve the roots thereof that they perish not, that I might preserve them unto myself, I have done this thing.—
Wherefore, go thy way; watch the tree, and nourish it, according to my words.

And these will I place in the nethermost part of my vineyard, whithersoever I will, it mattereth not unto thee; and I do it, that I may preserve unto myself the natural branches of the tree; and also, that I may lay up fruit thereof, against the season, unto myself: for it grieveth me that I should lose this tree, and the fruit thereof.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard went his way, and hid the natural branches of the tame olive tree in the nethermost parts of the vineyard; some in one, and some in another, according to his will and pleasure.
And it came to pass that a long time passed away, and the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant, Come, let us go down into the vineyard, that we may labor in the vineyard.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard, and also the servant, went down into the vineyard to labor. And it came to pass that the servant sayeth unto his master, Behold, look here; behold the tree.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard looked and beheld the tree, in the which the wild olive branches had been grafted; and it had sprang forth, and began to bear fruit. And he beheld that it was good; and the fruit thereof was like unto the natural fruit.—

And he sayeth unto the servant, Behold, the branches of the wild tree hath taken hold of the moisture of the root thereof, that the root thereof hath brought forth much strength; and because of the much strength of the root thereof, the wild branches hath brought forth tame fruit: now, if we had not grafted in these branches, the tree thereof would have perished. And now, behold, I shall lay up much fruit, which the tree thereof hath brought forth; and the fruit thereof I shall lay up, against the season, unto mine own self.

links.text: Boast not against the branches. But if thou boast, thou bearest not the root, but the root thee.

provenance.other: No distinctive phrase is reproduced; the terms shared with Romans 11:18 are 'root' and 'branches', both common. What is not common is the proposition — that the root carries the grafted branch and not the reverse — which the Bible states only here.
provenance.significance: Paul warns the grafted wild branch not to boast against the natural ones, because 'thou bearest not the root, but the root thee'. Jacob 5:18 is that sentence turned into narrative fact: the wild branches bear tame fruit only 'because of the much strength of the root thereof'. Then the allegory does what Paul only threatens. At 5:37 the wild branches 'have overran the roots thereof', at 5:48 the servant diagnoses the ruin as branches overcoming the roots, and at 5:65-66 the remedy is to keep root and top equal in strength so that neither overpowers the other. The catalogue's claim at 1 Nephi 10:12 was that Romans 11 is this book's master allegory; this is the row where Romans 11 supplies not a phrase but a mechanism.

links.note: 'The branches of the wild tree hath taken hold of the moisture of the root thereof, that the root thereof hath brought forth much strength; and because of the much strength of the root thereof, the wild branches hath brought forth tame fruit.' There is no wording to count here, which is why kjvSpecific is left uncertain and the subtype is conceptual. The claim is that the chapter's whole physiology of root and branch, including the disaster at 5:37-48 and the balancing rule at 5:66, is an exposition of one sentence of Paul that has no other biblical statement.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto the servant, Come, let us go to the nethermost part of the vineyard, and behold if the natural branches of the tree hath not brought forth much fruit also, that I may lay up of the fruit thereof, against the season, unto mine own self.

And it came to pass that they went forth whither the master of the vineyard had hid the natural branches of the tree, and he sayeth unto the servant, Behold these: and he beheld the first, that it had brought forth much fruit; and he beheld also, that it was good. And he sayeth unto the servant, Take of the fruit thereof, and lay it up, against the season, that I may preserve it unto mine own self: for behold, sayeth he, This long time have I nourished it, and it hath brought forth much fruit.

And it came to pass that the servant sayeth unto his master, How comest thou hither to plant this tree, or this branch of the tree? for behold, it was the poorest spot in all the land of thy vineyard.

And the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto him, Counsel me not: I knew that it was a poor spot of ground; wherefore, I said unto thee, I have nourished it this long time; and thou beholdest that it hath brought forth much fruit.

links.text: For who hath known the mind of the Lord? or who hath been his counsellor?
links.whyNot: Two words, and common ones. 'Counsel me not' shares nothing distinctive with Romans 11:34 beyond the root 'counsel', and a master rebuking a servant for second-guessing him needs no source. The row rests entirely on position: the rebuke stands inside an allegory built out of Romans 11, at the point where the servant questions the Lord's choice of ground.

provenance.route: Romans 11:34 (quoting Isaiah 40:13) → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “his counsellor” occurs in eight KJV verses, so nothing here is decided by rarity. Romans 11:34 quotes Isaiah 40:13, and mediation cannot be settled: tools/mediation-check.py finds no point where the two versions differ that the Book of Mormon's two words reproduce.
provenance.significance: Romans 11 ends by forbidding exactly the question the servant asks. Paul closes the olive-tree argument with 'who hath been his counsellor?', and Jacob 5's servant, having asked why the Lord planted in the poorest spot of ground, is told 'Counsel me not'. If the allegory is an expansion of Romans 11 — which 5:7 and 5:18 argue — then it has expanded the doxology too, and made the unanswerable question into a scene.

links.note: 'Counsel me not: I knew that it was a poor spot of ground.' Recorded at moderate as a positional echo rather than a verbal one. Compare Romans 9:20 for the same rebuke in a different figure. The interest is that this chapter's only moment of friction between servant and master falls where Romans 11's own argument runs out.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant, Look hither: behold, I have planted another branch of the tree also; and thou knowest that this spot of ground was poorer than the first, But, behold the tree: I have nourished it this long time, and it hath brought forth much fruit; therefore, gather it, and lay it up, against the season, that I may preserve it unto mine own self.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth again unto his servant, Look hither, and behold another branch also, which I have planted: behold that I have nourished it also, and it hath brought forth fruit.

And he sayeth unto the servant, Look hither, and behold the last: behold, this have I planted in a good spot of ground; and I have nourished it this long time, and only a part of the tree hath brought forth tame fruit; and the other part of the tree hath brought forth wild fruit: behold, I have nourished this tree like unto the others.
And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto the servant, Pluck off the branches that have not brought forth good fruit, and cast them into the fire.

links.text: Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away: and every branch that beareth fruit, he purgeth it, that it may bring forth more fruit.

provenance.other: “beareth not fruit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “every branch in me” in exactly one, both John 15:2; “and they are burned” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 15:6, whose 'men gather them, and cast them into the fire' is the source of this chapter's standing formula.
provenance.significance: John 15 is the one place in the KJV where the owner of the plant is the Father, the pruning is his own act, and the removed branches are gathered and burned — which is precisely the division of labour in Jacob 5, and precisely what Isaiah 5 and Luke 13 do not supply (Isaiah's owner destroys the whole vineyard; Luke's owner delegates to a hired dresser). 1 Nephi 15:15 had already put John's vine beside Paul's olive tree in a single sentence; here the two are fused for seventy-seven verses, and the seam shows only in the vocabulary.

links.note: 'Pluck off the branches that have not brought forth good fruit, and cast them into the fire.' Both halves are KJV singletons from the same passage: John 15:2's branch that beareth not fruit and is taken away, John 15:6's branches cast into the fire and burned. The Book of Mormon's formula 'cast them into the fire' recurs at 5:7, 5:9, 5:42, 5:49, 5:58 and 5:66, and John 15:6 is one of only two KJV verses to contain it. Matthew 7:19 supplies the other governing form, 'bringeth not forth good fruit … hewn down, and cast into the fire', which is catalogued separately at 5:42.

pericopes.text: But behold, the servant sayeth unto him, Let us prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it a little longer, that perhaps it may bring forth good fruit unto thee, that thou canst lay it up against the season.—

links.text: And if it bear fruit, well: and if not, then after that thou shalt cut it down.

provenance.other: “let it alone this year” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 13:8, and it is the only reprieve granted to a tree anywhere in the Bible. The whole conditional shape — one more term of cultivation, then the axe if nothing comes — exists only at Luke 13:8-9.
provenance.significance: The servant's intercession is the structural engine of Jacob 5, and it is Luke's invention. Three times an owner resolves to destroy and three times a servant asks for delay (5:27, 5:50, and by implication 5:34), and each time the delay is granted on Luke's terms: more labour now, judgment deferred. Metalepsis in the strict sense — the point of the borrowing lies in what Luke 13:9 says next and Jacob 5 does not, that if the tree still fails 'then after that thou shalt cut it down', which is what 5:42 and 5:49 finally propose.

links.note: 'Let us prune it, and dig about it, and nourish it a little longer, that perhaps it may bring forth good fruit unto thee.' The servant's speech reproduces the dresser's: cultivation named in the same order, a probationary period, and a conditional hope of fruit. At 5:50 it shortens to 'Spare it a little longer', and the Lord grants it in the same words at 5:51. No clause is reproduced verbatim, but the scene is Luke's scene and its vocabulary was already shown to be Luke's at 5:4.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard, and the servant of the Lord of the vineyard, did nourish all the fruit of the vineyard.

And it came to pass that a long time had passed away, and the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant, Come, let us go down into the vineyard, that we may labor again in the vineyard. For behold, the time draweth near, and the end soon cometh: wherefore, I must lay up fruit, against the season, unto mine own self.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard, and the servant, went down into the vineyard; and they came to the tree whose natural branches had been broken off, and the wild branches had been grafted in; and behold, all sorts of fruit did cumber the tree.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard did taste of the fruit, every sort according to its number. And the Lord of the vineyard saith, Behold, this long time have we nourished this tree, and I have laid up unto myself against the season, much fruit.

But behold, this time it hath brought forth much fruit, and there is none of it which is good. And behold, there are all kinds of bad fruit; and it profiteth me nothing, notwithstanding all our labor: and now, it grieveth me that I should lose this tree.

links.text: And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.

provenance.other: “profiteth me nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Corinthians 13:3.
provenance.significance: The verdict on the vineyard is delivered in the phrase Paul reserves for works done without charity. Both sentences describe an expenditure of labour that yields a return the speaker cannot use — 'notwithstanding all our labor' answers 'though I bestow all my goods' — and in both the failure is not of quantity but of kind.

links.note: 'It profiteth me nothing, notwithstanding all our labor.' A four-word KJV singleton in a sentence about fruitless effort, which is 1 Corinthians 13:3's subject. Held at moderate: the phrase is ordinary English as well as Pauline English, and the sense is not distinctively Paul's. It is recorded because the count is absolute and the surrounding clause about labour spent for nothing sharpens it.

pericopes.text: And the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto the servant, What shall we do unto the tree, that I may preserve again good fruit thereof unto mine own self?

And the servant sayeth unto his master, Behold, because thou didst graft in the branches of the wild olive tree, they have nourished the roots, that they are alive, and they have not perished; wherefore, thou beholdest that they are yet good.
And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant, The tree profiteth me nothing; and the roots thereof profiteth me nothing, so long as it shall bring forth evil fruit.

links.text: Yet all this availeth me nothing, so long as I see Mordecai the Jew sitting at the king’s gate.

provenance.other: “availeth me nothing” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The construction it belongs to — a verb of profit, 'me nothing', and a 'so long as' clause naming the single thing that spoils an otherwise complete satisfaction — occurs nowhere else in the Authorized Version.
provenance.significance: Haman has just recited his honours and finds them worthless while one man sits unbowed at the gate; the Lord of the vineyard has just been told his roots are alive and finds them worthless while the tree bears evil fruit. The syntax carries the psychology: a grievance that cannot be answered by any addition, only by the removal of the one thing. It is the least likely source in the chapter and the most exactly matched sentence-shape in it.

links.note: 'The tree profiteth me nothing; and the roots thereof profiteth me nothing, so long as it shall bring forth evil fruit.' The n-gram stream proposed Esther 5:13 here on the runs 'me nothing so long' and 'nothing so long as', and on reading it holds: the KJV has exactly one sentence of this shape. The 1830 reading matters. The first edition writes 'the roots thereof profiteth me nothing', with Esther's singular verb; the 1920 edition changed the second verb to 'profit' and broke the parallel, so the borrowing is plainer in the running text than in the modern one.

pericopes.text: Nevertheless, I know that the roots are good; and for mine own purpose I have preserved them; and because of their much strength, they have hitherto brought forth from the wild branches, good fruit.

But behold, the wild branches have grown, and have overran the roots thereof; and because that the wild branches have overcome the roots thereof, it hath brought forth much evil fruit; and because that it hath brought forth so much evil fruit, thou beholdest that it begineth to perish: and it will soon become ripened, that it may be cast into the fire, except we should do something for it to preserve it.

And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto his servant, Let us go down into the nethermost parts of the vineyard, and behold if the natural branches have also brought forth evil fruit.

And it came to pass that they went down into the nethermost parts of the vineyard. And it came to pass that they beheld that the fruit of the natural branches had become corrupt also; yea, the first, and the second, and also the last; and they had all become corrupt.
And the wild fruit of the last, had overcome that part of the tree which brought forth good fruit, even that the branch had withered away and died.
And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard wept, and sayeth unto the servant, What could I have done more for my vineyard?

links.text: What could have been done more to my vineyard, that I have not done in it? wherefore, when I looked that it should bring forth grapes, brought it forth wild grapes?

provenance.other: “what could have been done more” occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon puts the question in the first person and the active voice — 'What could I have done more for my vineyard?' — which is the only substantive change; every content word is Isaiah's, in Isaiah's order.
provenance.significance: The sentence is asked three times in this chapter (5:41, 5:47, 5:49), and each time it is asked it does more of Isaiah's work. At 5:41 it is the lament; at 5:47 it is answered item by item, which is what Isaiah 5:4 only implies ('that I have not done in it'); at 5:49 it justifies the sentence of destruction, which is Isaiah 5:5-6. And Isaiah 5:7 supplies the identification the allegory opened with at 5:3: 'the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel'. Isaiah asks the question and moves immediately to destruction; Zenos asks it and then refuses to act on it for another thirty verses. That refusal is the whole argument of Jacob 5, and it is legible only against Isaiah 5.

links.note: 'And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard wept, and sayeth unto the servant, What could I have done more for my vineyard?' A complete clause reproduced from a KJV singleton, with the voice changed from passive to first-person active. Far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not among his catalogued quotations; it is entered as a quotation on the strength of the absolute rarity and of the surrounding structure, which is Isaiah 5:1-7 in sequence. Isaiah's owner does not weep, and the tear is the allegory's addition.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

pericopes.text: Behold, I knew that all the fruit of the vineyard, save it were these, had become corrupted. And now, these which have once brought forth good fruit, have also become corrupted. And now, all the trees of my vineyard are good for nothing, save it be to be hewn down and cast into the fire.

links.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: “hewn down” occurs in five KJV verses and “cast into the fire” in five; the three that contain both are Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9, and all three say it of a tree that brings forth no good fruit. “good for nothing” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Jeremiah 13:10 and Matthew 5:13.
provenance.significance: The sentence Jacob 5 passes on the vineyard is the Baptist's sentence, and Matthew 7:19 is the shortest form of it. What the borrowing brings with it is the axe already laid to the root (Matthew 3:10, Luke 3:9), which is why the chapter's crisis is a crisis about roots. Note also that 'good for nothing, save it be to be hewn down' fuses Matthew 5:13's verdict on savourless salt with the Baptist's verdict on fruitless trees — two judgment sayings from the same Gospel, welded at the seam.

links.note: 'All the trees of my vineyard are good for nothing, save it be to be hewn down and cast into the fire.' The n-gram stream ranks this run at 5:42, 5:46 and 5:66, and it is a genuine seven-word agreement with a formula the KJV states three times. Adjudicated here at first full use; the later occurrences are the chapter reusing its own borrowed formula.

pericopes.text: And behold, this last, whose branch hath withered away, I did plant in a good spot of ground; yea, even that which was choice unto me, above all other parts of the land of my vineyard.

links.text: And he fenced it, and gathered out the stones thereof, and planted it with the choicest vine, and built a tower in the midst of it, and also made a winepress therein: and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes.

provenance.other: “fruitful hill” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “gathered out the stones” in exactly one and “choicest vine” in exactly one, all of them Isaiah 5:1-2.
provenance.significance: Isaiah's owner does three things before planting: he takes very good ground, clears what is in it, and puts in the choicest stock. Jacob 5:43-44 does the same three in the same order — a spot 'choice unto me, above all other parts of the land', then 'I also cut down that which cumbered this spot of ground, that I might plant this tree in the stead thereof'. And the outcome is Isaiah's outcome, stated in Isaiah's antithesis: part brought forth good fruit and part wild fruit, where Isaiah looked for grapes and got wild grapes. This is the passage of the chapter that is closest to being a retelling rather than an allusion.

links.note: 'This last, whose branch hath withered away, I did plant in a good spot of ground; yea, even that which was choice unto me, above all other parts of the land of my vineyard.' No phrase is reproduced, but the sequence of preparation is Isaiah 5:2's and the disappointment is Isaiah 5:2's, and the chapter has already quoted Isaiah 5:4 two verses earlier. Held at moderate because the three rarity counts belong to words the Book of Mormon does not use — it says 'choice' for 'choicest', 'cut down that which cumbered' for 'gathered out the stones'.
bibliography: Hardy MSI at Jacob 4.3 (Isaiah 5:1-7, Luke 13:6-9, Romans 11:17-24)

pericopes.text: And thou beheldest that I also cut down that which cumbered this spot of ground, that I might plant this tree in the stead thereof.

And thou beheldest that a part thereof, brought forth good fruit; and a part thereof, brought forth wild fruit. And because that I plucked not the branches thereof, and cast them into the fire, behold, they have overcome the good branch, that it hath withered away.

And now behold, notwithstanding all the care which we have taken of my vineyard, the trees thereof hath become corrupted, that they bring forth no good fruit; and these I had hope to preserve, to have laid up fruit thereof, against the season, unto mine own self. But behold, they have become like unto the wild olive tree; and they are of no worth, but to be hewn down and cast into the fire: and it grieveth me that I should lose them.

But what could I have done more in my vineyard? Have I slackened mine hand, that I have not nourished it? Nay; I have nourished it, and I have digged it, and I have pruned it, and I have dunged it; and I have stretched forth mine hand almost all the day long; and the end draweth nigh. And it grieveth me that I should hew down all the trees of my vineyard, and cast them into the fire, that they should be burned. Who is it that hath corrupted my vineyard?

links.text: But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:2 → Romans 10:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “spread out my hands” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Ezra 9:5 and Isaiah 65:2. Romans 10:21 quotes Isaiah 65:2 and changes its verb: the Old Testament has 'I have spread out my hands all the day', the New Testament has 'All day long I have stretched forth my hands'. tools/mediation-check.py reports one decisive divergence and the Book of Mormon is on the New Testament side of it.
provenance.alternative: Isaiah 65:2, if 'stretched forth' is treated as a natural English variation rather than a borrowing. The word order tells against that: 'all the day long' keeps Isaiah's 'all the day' and adds Paul's 'long', so the clause is a hybrid, and a hybrid presupposes both texts.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's mediation test and it resolves cleanly. Where the KJV Old Testament and the KJV New Testament word the same sentence differently, Jacob 5:47 has the New Testament's word — 'stretched forth', not 'spread out' — which places it with the sixteen OT-via-NT rows that were the 1 Nephi pilot's principal result. What comes with Romans 10:21 is its addressee: Paul's 'But to Israel he saith' is the header of the quotation, and Jacob 5 is Zenos speaking to the house of Israel. Isaiah 65:2 has the same sense but not the same audience marked in the verse.

links.note: 'I have stretched forth mine hand almost all the day long; and the end draweth nigh.' The verse is a knot of three sources: Isaiah 5:4's question opens it ('what could I have done more in my vineyard?'), Luke 13:8's verbs fill its middle ('I have digged it … I have dunged it'), and its climax is Romans 10:21. The mediation is decided by one word. Isaiah 65:2 reads 'spread out', Romans 10:21 reads 'stretched forth', and the Book of Mormon reads 'stretched forth'. The one change the Book of Mormon makes is its own: it inserts 'almost', which neither source has, and which converts a complaint of unlimited patience into a patience that is running out — the point the next clause makes explicit.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the servant, sayeth unto his master, Is it not the loftiness of thy vineyard? Hath not the branches thereof overcame the roots, which are good? And because that the branches have overcame the roots thereof? For behold, they grew faster than the strength of the roots thereof, taking strength unto themselves. Behold, I say, Is not this the cause that the trees of thy vineyard hath become corrupted?

links.text: And the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low: and the LORD alone shall be exalted in that day.

provenance.other: “loftiness” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Isaiah 2:17 and Jeremiah 48:29, and in both it means pride, not height, and in both it is about to be brought down.
provenance.significance: The servant's diagnosis of the vineyard uses a word the Authorized Version reserves for the arrogance that the day of the Lord humbles. That is a moral term inserted into what is otherwise a purely horticultural explanation — the branches grew faster than the roots could bear — and it is the only place in seventy-seven verses where the allegory names the failure as a sin rather than as a botanical accident.

links.note: 'Is it not the loftiness of thy vineyard? Hath not the branches thereof overcame the roots, which are good?' The 1830 reading is 'overcame' where 1920 reads 'overcome'. Held at moderate: one word, and the Book of Mormon's syntax is its own. The case is that the word is rare, that both its KJV occurrences carry the same moral charge, and that it does work here no other word in the sentence does. Compare Romans 11:18 at 5:18 — Paul forbids the grafted branch to boast against the root, and this is that boast succeeding.

pericopes.text: And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto the servant, Let us go to, and hew down the trees of the vineyard, and cast them into the fire, that they shall not cumber the ground of my vineyard; for I have done all: what could I have done more for my vineyard?
But behold, the servant saith unto the Lord of the vineyard, Spare it a little longer.
And the Lord saith, Yea, I will spare it a little longer: for it grieveth me that I should lose the trees of my vineyard.

Wherefore, let us take of the branches of these which I have planted in the nethermost parts of my vineyard, and let us graft them into the tree from whence they came; and let us pluck from the tree, those branches whose fruit is most bitter, and graft in the natural branches of the tree, in the stead thereof.
And this will I do, that the tree may not perish, that perhaps I may preserve unto myself the roots thereof, for mine own purpose.

And behold, the roots of the natural branches of the tree which I planted whithersoever I would, are yet alive; wherefore, that I may preserve them also, for mine own purpose, I will take of the branches of this tree, and I will graft them in unto them. Yea, I will graft in unto them the branches of their mother tree, that I may preserve the roots also unto mine own self, that when they shall be sufficiently strong, that perhaps they may bring forth good fruit unto me, and I may yet have glory in the fruit of my vineyard.
And it came to pass that they took from the natural tree which had become wild, and grafted in unto the natural trees, which also had become wild;
and they also took of the natural trees which had become wild, and grafted into their mother tree.

And the Lord of the vineyard sayeth unto the servant, Pluck not the wild branches from the trees, save it be those which are most bitter; and in them ye shall graft, according to that which I have said.

And we will nourish again the trees of the vineyard, and we will trim up the branches thereof; and we will pluck from the trees those branches which are ripened, that must perish, and cast them into the fire.—
And this I do, that perhaps the roots thereof may take strength, because of their goodness; and because of the change of the branches, that the good may overcome the evil;

and because that I have preserved the natural branches, and the roots thereof; and that I have grafted in the natural branches again, into their mother tree; and have preserved the roots of their mother tree, that perhaps the trees of my vineyard may bring forth again good fruit; and that I may have joy again in the fruit of my vineyard; and perhaps that I may rejoice exceedingly, that I have preserved the roots and the branches of the first fruit;

wherefore, go to, and call servants, that we may labor diligently with our mights in the vineyard, that we may prepare the way, that I may bring forth again the natural fruit, which natural fruit is good, and the most precious above all other fruit.
Wherefore, let us go to, and labor with our mights, this last time: for behold, the end draweth nigh; and this is for the last time that I shall prune my vineyard.

Graft in the branches: begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last, and dig about the trees, both old and young, the first and the last, and the last and the first, that all may be nourished once again for the last time.

links.text: So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.

provenance.other: “the last shall be first” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 19:30 and Matthew 20:16, and both belong to the same discourse. “beginning from the last” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:8, and “labourers into his vineyard” in exactly one, Matthew 20:1.
provenance.significance: This is where the borrowing catalogued at 5:8 pays out. The title 'Lord of the vineyard' came from Matthew 20:8; Matthew 20:8's own sentence continues 'beginning from the last unto the first', and Matthew 20:16 draws the moral 'the last shall be first, and the first last'. Jacob 5:63 has both halves — 'begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last' — applied not to wages but to grafting order. Recover the parable and the reading changes: in Matthew the reversal is a scandal to the labourers hired first, and here it is simply the method by which the vineyard is saved. The allegory has taken Matthew's most contested saying and made it a horticultural instruction.

links.note: 'Graft in the branches: begin at the last, that they may be first, and that the first may be last, and dig about the trees, both old and young, the first and the last, and the last and the first.' The saying is diffused across four KJV verses (Matthew 19:30, 20:16, Mark 10:31, Luke 13:30) and would be weak evidence alone; what makes the case is that this chapter has already taken its name for God from the one parable in which the saying is worked out with labourers, a vineyard, and a payment order that literally begins from the last. The n-gram stream proposed Revelation 1:11 here on 'the first and the last', which is the wrong source — see the exclusion register.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, dig about them, and prune them, and dung them once more, for the last time: for the end draweth nigh. And if it so be that these last grafts shall grow, and bring forth the natural fruit, then shall ye prepare the way for them, that they may grow;

and as they begin to grow, ye shall clear away the branches which bring forth bitter fruit, according to the strength of the good and the size thereof; and ye shall not clear away the bad thereof, all at once, lest the roots thereof should be too strong for the graft, and the graft thereof shall perish, and I lose the trees of my vineyard.

links.text: But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them.

provenance.other: “lest while ye gather” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “root up also the wheat” in exactly one, both Matthew 13:29. No word of either is reproduced, which is why kjvSpecific is left uncertain; what is reproduced is the argument, which the Bible makes only here.
provenance.significance: Matthew 13:29 is the one place in scripture where evil is left standing on purpose, and for a stated reason: uprooting it now would take the good with it. Jacob 5:65 gives that reason a mechanism — clear the bad away too fast and the roots will overpower the graft — and 5:66 gives it a rule, that the root and the top be kept equal in strength. Then 5:77 ends the allegory where Matthew 13:30 ends the parable, with a final separation of good from bad at the harvest. The Book of Mormon has taken the parable of the tares and rewritten it as horticulture.

links.note: 'Ye shall not clear away the bad thereof, all at once, lest the roots thereof should be too strong for the graft, and the graft thereof shall perish.' The verbal contact is one word, 'lest'. The case for the link is the reasoning: a delayed purge, justified by the risk to the good, which is Matthew 13:29's proposition and no other verse's. Recorded at high because that proposition is distinctive and because the chapter closes on Matthew 13's harvest imagery at 5:77.

pericopes.text: For it grieveth me that I should lose the trees of my vineyard; wherefore, ye shall clear away the bad, according as the good shall grow, that the root and the top may be equal in strength, until the good shall overcome the bad, and the bad be hewn down and cast into the fire, that they cumber not the ground of my vineyard; and thus will I sweep away the bad out of my vineyard.
And the branches of the natural tree, will I graft in again, into the natural tree;

and the branches of the natural tree, will I graft into the natural branches of the tree; and thus will I bring them together again, that they shall bring forth the natural fruit: and they shall be one.

links.text: Say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I will take the stick of Joseph, which is in the hand of Ephraim, and the tribes of Israel his fellows, and will put them with him, even with the stick of Judah, and make them one stick, and they shall be one in mine hand.

provenance.other: “they shall be one” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 2:24 and Ezekiel 37:19. Genesis is about marriage; Ezekiel is about two separated portions of Israel joined in the Lord's hand, which is the subject of this verse. “one fold” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 10:16, already catalogued at 1 Nephi 15:15.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 37's two sticks — Joseph's and Judah's — made one in the Lord's hand is the Book of Mormon's own charter text for what it takes itself to be, and Jacob 5 ends by performing it: branches scattered to the nethermost parts are grafted back into the mother tree until 'they shall be one' and, at 5:74, 'they became like unto one body'. The allegory's addition to Romans 11 was always the hidden branches; Ezekiel is where the hidden branch has a name.

links.note: 'Thus will I bring them together again, that they shall bring forth the natural fruit: and they shall be one.' Three common words, and the count is only two — but the two are Genesis's marriage and Ezekiel's reunification, and only one of those is about Israel divided and restored. Held at moderate on that basis. The 'one body' of 5:74 pulls in the Pauline figure as well, which is why the composite names John 10:16's fold rather than settling on a single image: the chapter is assembling every KJV figure for incorporation, exactly as 1 Nephi 15:15 does in one sentence.

pericopes.text: And the bad shall be cast away; yea, even out of all the land of my vineyard: for behold, only this once will I prune my vineyard.
And it came to pass that the Lord of the vineyard sent his servant; and the servant went and did as the Lord had commanded him, and brought other servants; and they were few.

links.text: Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;

provenance.other: “the labourers are few” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 9:37 and Luke 10:2, and both are the same saying. “labourers into his vineyard” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 20:1.
provenance.significance: The sentence in Matthew is a call for more workers because the ones available cannot cover the harvest, and the sentence in Jacob 5 is the same shortage answered the same way: the servant is sent for others and comes back with few, and the Lord of the vineyard then labours alongside them (5:72). The one thing the Book of Mormon adds is the master in the field, which neither Matthew 9 nor Matthew 20 has.

links.note: 'The servant went and did as the Lord had commanded him, and brought other servants; and they were few.' The clause is not reproduced — 'they were few' against 'the labourers are few' — but the situation is the KJV's, and 5:71's 'Go to, and labor in the vineyard' returns to the hiring of Matthew 20:1. Recorded at moderate; the shortage of labourers is a natural thing to say, and the count of two is what keeps it in the catalogue.

pericopes.text: And the Lord of the vineyard saith unto them, Go to, and labor in the vineyard, with your mights. For behold, this is the last time that I shall nourish my vineyard: for the end is nigh at hand, and the season speedily cometh; and if ye labor with your mights with me, ye shall have joy in the fruit which I shall lay up unto myself, against the time which will soon come.

And it came to pass that the servants did go to it, and labor with their mights; and the Lord of the vineyard labored also with them: and they did obey the commandments of the Lord of the vineyard, in all things.

And there began to be the natural fruit again in the vineyard; and the natural branches began to grow and thrive exceedingly; and the wild branches began to be plucked off, and to be cast away; and they did keep the root and the top thereof, equal, according to the strength thereof.

And thus they labored, with all diligence, according to the commandments of the Lord of the vineyard, even until the bad had been cast away out of the vineyard, and the Lord had preserved unto himself, that the trees had become again the natural fruit; and they became like unto one body; and the fruit were equal; and the Lord of the vineyard had preserved unto himself the natural fruit, which was most precious unto him from the beginning.

And it came to pass that when the Lord of the vineyard saw that his fruit was good, and that his vineyard was no more corrupt, he calleth up his servants and sayeth unto them, Behold, for this last time have we nourished my vineyard; and thou beholdest that I have done according to my will; and I have preserved the natural fruit, that it is good, even like as it was in the beginning; and blessed art thou. For because that ye have been diligent in laboring with me in my vineyard, and have kept my commandments, and hath brought unto me again the natural fruit, that my vineyard is no more corrupted, and the bad is cast away, behold, ye shall have joy with me, because of the fruit of my vineyard.

links.text: His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.

provenance.other: “thou good and faithful servant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 25:21, and “the joy of thy lord” in exactly two, Matthew 25:21 and 25:23, which are the same commendation spoken twice.
provenance.significance: The allegory ends with the scene the KJV keeps for the end of the world: a lord returning, finding his servants diligent, and admitting them to his own joy. But the Book of Mormon changes the preposition and the direction. Matthew's servant is told to 'enter thou into the joy of thy lord'; Zenos's servants are told 'ye shall have joy with me' — joy shared in the field rather than joy entered as a reward, which is consistent with 5:72, where the Lord of the vineyard has been labouring beside them. The commendation formula is Matthew's; the fellowship in it is not.

links.note: 'Blessed art thou. For because that ye have been diligent in laboring with me in my vineyard, and have kept my commandments … ye shall have joy with me, because of the fruit of my vineyard.' A commendation for diligence over a long stewardship, ending in the lord's joy — Matthew 25:21 without the reproduced clause. The 1830 text reads 'he calleth up his servants and sayeth unto them' and keeps the singular 'blessed art thou' inside a plural address, a rough seam the later editions did not smooth.

pericopes.text: For behold, for a long time will I lay up of the fruit of my vineyard unto mine own self, against the season, which speedily cometh; and for the last time have I nourished my vineyard, and pruned it, and dug about it, and dunged it; wherefore I will lay up unto mine own self of the fruit, for a long time, according to that which I have spoken.

And when the time cometh that evil fruit shall again come into my vineyard, then will I cause the good and the bad to be gathered; and the good will I preserve unto myself; and the bad will I cast away into its own place. And then cometh the season and the end; and my vineyard will I cause to be burned with fire.

links.text: Which, when it was full, they drew to shore, and sat down, and gathered the good into vessels, but cast the bad away.

provenance.other: “gathered the good” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “cast the bad away” occurs in exactly one, both Matthew 13:48. The pairing of 'the good' and 'the bad' as the two halves of a final sorting exists nowhere else in the Authorized Version.
provenance.significance: The last verse of the allegory is Matthew 13's parable chapter compressed. The dragnet supplies the sorting — the good gathered and kept, the bad cast away; the tares supply the burning at the end of the age, 'as therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world' (13:40); and 13:49's 'So shall it be at the end of the world' supplies the timetable that Zenos states as 'then cometh the season and the end'. Read back into the chapter, this is what makes 5:65's delayed purge intelligible: the allegory has been running Matthew 13 from the tares to the dragnet, and it ends where Matthew ends.

links.note: 'Then will I cause the good and the bad to be gathered; and the good will I preserve unto myself; and the bad will I cast away into its own place. And then cometh the season and the end; and my vineyard will I cause to be burned with fire.' Two KJV singletons split across one sentence, in Matthew's order, with 'preserve' substituted for 'gathered … into vessels' — the chapter's own word, used thirteen times before this. The n-gram stream proposed Jeremiah 38:23 here for 'to be burned with fire', which is the wrong source; see the exclusion register.

pericopes.text: And now, behold, my brethren, as I said unto you that I would prophesy, behold, this is my prophesy: That the things which this prophet Zenos spake, concerning the House of Israel, in the which he likened them unto a tame olive tree, must surely come to pass.

links.text: For if thou wert cut out of the olive tree which is wild by nature, and wert graffed contrary to nature into a good olive tree: how much more shall these, which be the natural branches, be graffed into their own olive tree?

provenance.other: 'Good olive tree' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 11:24, where it stands against 'the olive tree which is wild by nature'. 'Tame olive tree' occurs in none. The wild/tame antithesis that governs Jacob 5 and is named here is Paul's wild/good antithesis with one term reworded.
provenance.significance: This verse is the seam. Jacob has just transcribed seventy-seven verses of Zenos and now, in his own voice, tells the reader what the allegory was: the house of Israel likened unto a tame olive tree. The Bible has exactly one olive-tree allegory of branches broken off, a wild stock grafted in, and the natural branches grafted back, and it is Romans 11 — already catalogued behind 1 Nephi 10:12 and quoted outright at 1 Nephi 15:13. What Jacob 6:1 adds is the word 'tame', which is not in the KJV: Paul's opposite of 'wild by nature' is 'good', a moral term, and the Book of Mormon has replaced it with a husbandman's term. The allegory is thereby moved out of Paul's argument about merit and into the vineyard, where Jacob 5 needs it.

links.note: The argument for Romans 11 behind the Book of Mormon's olive tree was made at 1 Nephi 10:12 and completed at 15:13 with the KJV singleton 'the fulness of the Gentiles'; it is not restated here. What this verse contributes is the label. Jacob attributes the allegory to Zenos, a prophet the Bible does not contain, and the figure he attributes to him is the one figure of its kind the Bible does contain. The link is recorded at Jacob 6:1 rather than across Jacob 5 because 6:1 is where the text itself names the tree.

pericopes.text: And in the day that he shall set his hand again the second time to recover his people, is the day, yea, even the last time, that the servants of the Lord shall go forth in his power, to nourish and prune his vineyard; and after that, the end soon cometh.

links.text: And it shall come to pass in that day, that the Lord shall set his hand again the second time to recover the remnant of his people, which shall be left, from Assyria, and from Egypt, and from Pathros, and from Cush, and from Elam, and from Shinar, and from Hamath, and from the islands of the sea.

provenance.other: 'Set his hand again the second time to recover' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The Book of Mormon reproduces ten consecutive words of it and drops only 'the remnant of' before 'his people'.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 11:11 is the verse the Book of Mormon uses as its own timetable, and it is used here to date the allegory. Zenos ended with a final pruning and burning; Jacob says when that is: the day of Isaiah's second gathering. The elision matters. Isaiah recovers 'the remnant of his people, which shall be left' — a survivors' clause, and a small number — while Jacob recovers 'his people' entire. The verse also stands one line below Isaiah 11:10's ensign to the Gentiles and one above 11:12's gathering of the outcasts of Israel from the four corners of the earth, which is the scattering Jacob 5 has spent seventy-seven verses undoing.

links.note: 'And in the day that he shall set his hand again the second time to recover his people, is the day, yea, even the last time, that the servants of the Lord shall go forth in his power, to nourish and prune his vineyard.' A ten-word run out of a KJV singleton, which on the project's standard (CONVENTIONS §2) is a quotation whatever its length; note that it falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not among his. Isaiah 11 is quoted whole at 2 Nephi 21 and this clause is reused at 2 Nephi 25:17 ('restore his people') and 2 Nephi 29:1 ('recover my people'); Jacob's 'recover' is Isaiah's own verb, so this is the closest of the three to the KJV. The second half of the verse leaves Isaiah for Zenos: 'nourish and prune his vineyard' is Jacob 5's vocabulary, not the KJV's.

pericopes.text: And how blessed are they who have labored diligently in his vineyard; and how cursed are they which shall be cast out into their own place! And the world shall be burned with fire.

links.text: For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.

provenance.other: 'Root nor branch' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Burned with fire' occurs in seventeen and carries nothing by itself; the link rests on the pairing of the burning with the roots and branches across Jacob 6:3-4, which is the pairing Malachi 4:1 makes in a single sentence.
provenance.significance: Malachi's burning day leaves the wicked 'neither root nor branch'. Jacob's next sentence says that God 'remembereth the house of Israel, both roots and branches'. The two halves of Malachi 4:1 are here in Malachi's order with the second one reversed, and the reversal is the point: the verse that in the KJV describes total extirpation is turned into the ground of mercy. Malachi 4:2 then supplies what Jacob 6:4 goes on to say — the sun of righteousness arising with healing — so the reversal is not against Malachi but with him, one verse further down. This is metalepsis in the strict sense: the mercy of Jacob 6:4 is legible as mercy only if the reader recovers what Malachi 4:1 does to the roots and branches of the proud.

links.note: 'And how cursed are they which shall be cast out into their own place! And the world shall be burned with fire.' Read with 6:4 as one movement. The burning belongs to Zenos — Jacob 5:77 has the vineyard burned — but the roots-and-branches formula is not in Jacob 5 and is not ordinary English; it is Malachi's, inverted. Held at high rather than certain because 'both roots and branches' is a reversal rather than a reproduction, and a reversal can always be an accident of a common image.

links.text: For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah his pleasant plant: and he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry.

provenance.other: Isaiah 5:7 is the only KJV verse that states the equation the whole of Jacob 5-6 assumes: the vineyard is the house of Israel. 'Prune' occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Leviticus 25:3, 25:4, Isaiah 5:6); Isaiah 5:6 is the vineyard that shall not be pruned.
provenance.significance: Jacob 6:1 says the tree is the house of Israel; Jacob 6:2-3 says the vineyard is where the servants labour. The KJV states that identification once, in the song of the vineyard, and it states it as an indictment — the vineyard brought forth wild grapes and will be laid waste and not pruned. Zenos's allegory is Isaiah 5 with the verdict suspended: the vineyard is pruned again and again rather than abandoned. Jacob 6:3's blessed labourers and cursed outcasts are the sentence Isaiah 5:5-6 passed, reopened.

links.note: No wording is reproduced, and none is claimed. The link is recorded because the identification Jacob works from — vineyard equals house of Israel — has exactly one biblical source, and because the pruning vocabulary of 6:2 has its only vineyard-side KJV occurrence in the same passage. Proposed under CONVENTIONS §0a as worth a reader's attention.
links.whyNot: The vineyard-as-Israel figure is common enough in Jewish and Christian usage that a nineteenth-century writer need not have been reading Isaiah 5 to reach it, and the proximate model is in any case Jacob 5, which the text has just quoted at length. Nothing verbal survives.

pericopes.text: And how merciful is our God unto us: for he remembereth the House of Israel, both roots and branches; and he stretches forth his hands unto them, all the day long: and they are a stiffnecked, and a gainsaying people; but as many as will not harden their hearts, shall be saved in the Kingdom of God.

links.text: But to Israel he saith, All day long I have stretched forth my hands unto a disobedient and gainsaying people.

provenance.route: Isaiah 65:2 → Romans 10:21 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Isaiah 65:2 KJV: 'I have spread out my hands all the day unto a rebellious people, which walketh in a way that was not good, after their own thoughts.'
provenance.other: 'Stretched forth my hands' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 10:21. 'Gainsaying people' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Romans 10:21. 'Gainsaying' occurs in three (Acts 10:29, Romans 10:21, Jude 1:11) and in only one of them is it an adjective for Israel. Isaiah 65:2, the verse Paul is quoting, has neither word: it reads 'spread out' and 'rebellious'.
provenance.significance: This is the chapter's principal finding and it is a clean mediation result. Jacob 6:4 says God 'stretches forth his hands unto them, all the day long: and they are a stiffnecked, and a gainsaying people'. Both of the distinctive expressions are KJV singletons at Romans 10:21, and neither is available from Isaiah, which is the Old Testament verse Paul is quoting. The Book of Mormon has the New Testament's rendering of an Old Testament text. What follows from that is more interesting than the fact itself. Romans 10:21 is the last verse of Paul's argument that Israel has heard and refused; the very next sentence is 'Hath God cast away his people? God forbid' (11:1), and eleven verses later Paul is at the olive tree. Jacob 6 runs the same three moves in the same order — the allegory, the outstretched hands to a gainsaying people, and the conclusion that God has not cast them off — but arrives at Paul's stretched-out hands after the olive tree rather than before it. The chapter reads as Romans 10:21-11:24 rearranged around a longer allegory.

links.note: 'And he stretches forth his hands unto them, all the day long: and they are a stiffnecked, and a gainsaying people.' Note that tools/mediation-check.py could not decide this one and reported no decisive divergence: the Book of Mormon shifts Paul's first person into the third ('he stretches forth his hands' for 'I have stretched forth my hands'), which defeats a word-level aligner, and the tool therefore saw the Book of Mormon agreeing with neither candidate at every point. Adjudicated by eye against the rarity counts instead, which are unambiguous. Two independent KJV singletons from the same verse, plus 'all the day long', which is a hybrid: Romans has 'All day long', Isaiah has 'all the day', and the Book of Mormon's form is the one thirteen other KJV verses use. 'Stiffnecked' replaces Paul's 'disobedient' and is the Pentateuch's word for the same people (Exodus 32:9 and eight others). Held at high rather than certain only because no continuous clause survives the change of person.

pericopes.text: Wherefore, my beloved brethren, I beseech of you in words of soberness, that ye would repent, and come with full purpose of heart, and cleave unto God as he cleaveth unto you. And while his arm of mercy is extended towards you in the light of the day, harden not your hearts.

links.text: Who, when he came, and had seen the grace of God, was glad, and exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.

provenance.other: 'Purpose of heart' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. 'Cleave unto' occurs in thirteen, but Acts 11:23 is the only KJV verse that joins the two — purpose of heart and cleaving — and it joins them in Jacob's order, the purpose first and the cleaving after.
provenance.significance: Barnabas at Antioch, exhorting a congregation of new Gentile believers to hold fast, is the KJV's one model for the sentence Jacob is writing. The context is worth recovering. Acts 11 is the chapter in which the church discovers that God has granted repentance to the Gentiles, which is precisely the discovery Zenos's allegory dramatizes and Jacob 6:4 has just affirmed — that God remembers the whole tree. So the exhortation Jacob addresses to the natural branches is worded out of the exhortation Luke gives to the grafted ones. Note also what Jacob adds and the KJV does not have: 'as he cleaveth unto you'. In the Bible, cleaving is what Israel does to the Lord, never what the Lord does to Israel; Deuteronomy and Joshua use the verb thirteen times and always in that direction. Jacob makes it reciprocal, which is a theological move made by reversing a preposition.

links.note: 'That ye would repent, and come with full purpose of heart, and cleave unto God as he cleaveth unto you.' The KJV singleton plus the verb it governs, in order. The Deuteronomic cleaving formula (Deuteronomy 11:22, 30:20, Joshua 23:8) supplies the idiom's background but not the collocation with purpose of heart, which is Acts 11:23's alone.

links.text: But he said, I am not mad, most noble Festus; but speak forth the words of truth and soberness.

provenance.other: 'Soberness' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The collocation 'words of … soberness' occurs there and nowhere else.
provenance.significance: Paul says it to Festus, who has just shouted that much learning has made him mad. The words of soberness are a defence against the charge of raving. Jacob uses the phrase at the one point in his book where he most needs that defence: he has just read out seventy-seven verses of an allegory about a man and some olive branches, and he opens his application with 'I beseech of you in words of soberness'. Whether or not the borrowing is deliberate, the KJV supplies that phrase for exactly one rhetorical situation, and Jacob is in it.

links.note: A one-word KJV rarity carrying a two-word phrase. Held at moderate: 'soberness' is a natural English word and the Book of Mormon writer need not have had Acts 26 open. What raises it above coincidence is that the phrase's single KJV home is a plea not to be thought mad, and this is the sentence in which Jacob asks to be taken seriously.
links.whyNot: Two words. 'Soberness' is rare in the KJV but not rare in the English of 1830, and 'words of soberness' could be assembled without any source at all.

pericopes.text: Yea, to-day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts: for why will ye die?

links.text: Again, he limiteth a certain day, saying in David, To day, after so long a time; as it is said, To day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.

provenance.route: Psalm 95:7-8 → Hebrews 4:7 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Psalm 95:7-8 KJV: 'To day if ye will hear his voice, Harden not your heart, as in the provocation, and as in the day of temptation in the wilderness.'
provenance.other: 'Harden not your hearts', plural, occurs in exactly three KJV verses — Hebrews 3:8, 3:15 and 4:7 — and in no Old Testament verse. Psalm 95:8 reads the singular, 'Harden not your heart'. The Book of Mormon's twelve-word run therefore cannot come from the Psalm.
provenance.significance: A decisive mediation result on a single letter. Every English word Jacob 6:6 uses is in Psalm 95:7-8 except the 's' on 'hearts', and that 's' is the New Testament's. The choice between the three Hebrews verses is decidable too, and by the same method: Hebrews 3:8 and 3:15 both continue 'as in the provocation', and Hebrews 4:7 is the one place in the Bible where the quotation from the Psalm stops exactly where Jacob's stops, at 'harden not your hearts', with nothing after it. What the reader recovers by going back is Hebrews' argument about the word 'To day' — that God 'limiteth a certain day' and that the day is still open, which is the whole burden of Jacob 6:5's 'while his arm of mercy is extended towards you in the light of the day' in the sentence immediately before.

links.note: 'Yea, to-day if ye will hear his voice, harden not your hearts.' Twelve consecutive words. Below Skousen's threshold and not among his quotations, and catalogued here as a quotation on the criteria of CONVENTIONS §2. Note that tools/mediation-check.py returned no decisive divergence for this verse, because the KJV's versification puts 'To day if ye will hear his voice' at the end of Psalm 95:7 and 'Harden not your heart' at the beginning of 95:8, so a comparison against 95:7 alone never sees the singular that settles it; the rarity count does. The 1830 hyphenation 'to-day' matches the KJV's two-word 'To day' more closely than the modern edition's 'today' does — a small instance of CONVENTIONS §8.

links.text: Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel?

provenance.other: 'Why will ye die' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Jeremiah 27:13, where the death in question is by sword, famine and pestilence for refusing to serve Babylon, and Ezekiel 18:31 and 33:11, where it closes a call to repent. Only the Ezekiel pair is addressed to 'the house of Israel', which is the subject of Jacob 6 from its first verse.
provenance.significance: Ezekiel 18:31 pairs the question with the command to 'make you a new heart', and Jacob 6:6 pairs it with 'harden not your hearts'. The heart is the hinge in both. Ezekiel 33:11 supplies the reason the question is asked at all — 'I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked' — which is the mercy Jacob has just asserted at 6:4-5, so both Ezekiel passages are doing work here even though only one supplies the wording's setting.

links.note: 'For why will ye die?' Five words, and they arrive at the end of a sentence whose first twelve came from Hebrews 4:7. Jacob has stitched a New Testament exhortation to an Old Testament one and the join is invisible. Ezekiel rather than Jeremiah on the addressee: Jeremiah 27:13 threatens Zedekiah's court with a specific political death, while Ezekiel asks the house of Israel why it will not repent, and Jacob 6 is asking the second question.

pericopes.text: For behold, after that ye have been nourished by the good word of God all the day long, will ye bring forth evil fruit, that ye must be hewn down and cast into the fire?

links.text: And have tasted the good word of God, and the powers of the world to come,

provenance.other: 'The good word of God' occurs in exactly one KJV verse.
provenance.significance: The singleton is only the door. Recover the four verses around it and Jacob 6:7 turns out to be Hebrews 6:5-8 in Hebrews' own order. Hebrews: they have tasted the good word of God (6:5); if they shall fall away it is impossible to renew them to repentance (6:6); the ground that drinks the rain and bears herbs receives blessing (6:7); but that which beareth thorns and briers 'is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned' (6:8). Jacob: 'after that ye have been nourished by the good word of God all the day long, will ye bring forth evil fruit, that ye must be hewn down and cast into the fire?' The rare phrase, the falling away, the well-watered ground that bears the wrong thing, and the burning — four elements, one sequence, one paragraph of Hebrews. That the Book of Mormon reaches for Matthew 7's wording for the burning rather than Hebrews' own is what keeps this an allusion rather than a quotation.

links.note: 'After that ye have been nourished by the good word of God all the day long.' The KJV's one occurrence of the phrase, with Hebrews' 'tasted' replaced by 'nourished', which is Jacob 5's verb and the allegory's — the good word of God is thereby fed to the reader the way the servants fed the tree. 'All the day long' repeats from 6:4 and carries Romans 10:21's outstretched hands forward into the reproach. Held at high, not certain, because the phrase is short and the surrounding correspondence is structural rather than verbal.

links.text: Every tree that bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.

provenance.other: 'Hewn down, and cast into the fire' occurs in exactly three KJV verses: Matthew 3:10, Matthew 7:19 and Luke 3:9. The seven-word run alone cannot choose among them. 'Bring forth evil fruit' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 7:18, which stands immediately before Matthew 7:19 — and Jacob 6:7 has both. Neither Matthew 3:10 nor Luke 3:9 has a neighbouring verse with 'evil fruit'; both read 'bringeth not forth good fruit' and stop.
provenance.significance: A source chosen by a second rarity rather than by the long run, which is the method CONVENTIONS §9 recommends when the n-gram stream offers a tie. The consequence is not trivial. Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 are John the Baptist threatening the Pharisees with an axe already laid to the root; Matthew 7:18-19 is the Sermon on the Mount teaching a congregation how to tell false prophets by their fruit. Jacob 6:7-8 goes on to ask whether his hearers will 'reject the words of the prophets', so the Sermon's setting — how to judge a prophet — is the one his paragraph is in.

links.note: 'Will ye bring forth evil fruit, that ye must be hewn down and cast into the fire?' The singleton at Matthew 7:18 and the seven-word run at 7:19, adjacent in the KJV and adjacent here. The machine ranked Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 equal with Matthew 7:19, having nothing to break the tie; the tie breaks on 'evil fruit'. Recorded as a quotation on the seven-word run, well below Skousen's threshold and not among his.

pericopes.text: Behold, will ye reject these words? Will ye reject the words of the Prophets? and will ye reject all the words which have been spoken concerning Christ, after that so many have spoken concerning him? and deny the good word of Christ, and the power of God, and the gift of the Holy Ghost, and quench the Holy Spirit? and make a mock of the great plan of redemption, which hath been laid for you?

links.text: Quench not the Spirit.

provenance.other: 'Quench' occurs in thirty-one KJV verses, almost all of them literal — fire, coals, thirst, the smoking flax — and in exactly one of them is the object the Spirit. 'The gift of the Holy Ghost' occurs in exactly two, Acts 2:38 and Acts 10:45.
provenance.significance: Jacob 6:8 is a list of five refusals and every item on it is a New Testament phrase: the good word of Christ (Hebrews 6:5's phrase with Christ for God), the power of God, the gift of the Holy Ghost, the quenching of the Spirit, and the plan of redemption. The last is the only one that is not KJV at all — 'plan of redemption' occurs in no KJV verse — and it is the one Jacob is actually arguing for. So the sentence recruits four biblical phrases to lend their weight to a fifth that is the Book of Mormon's own coinage.

links.note: 'And quench the Holy Spirit.' The KJV forbids quenching the Spirit once; Jacob turns the prohibition into an accusation and expands 'the Spirit' to 'the Holy Spirit'. Note the two Acts phrases in the same breath: 'the gift of the Holy Ghost' is Peter's at Pentecost (Acts 2:38) and again at Cornelius's house (10:45), which are the two moments the New Testament reports the gift being given.

links.text: Fools make a mock at sin: but among the righteous there is favour.

provenance.other: 'Make a mock' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. The KJV elsewhere uses 'mock' as a verb with a direct object ('they mocked him'); the idiom 'make a mock at' is Proverbs 14:9's alone.
provenance.significance: The KJV's only mocker of this construction is a fool, and the thing he mocks is sin. Jacob's mocker mocks the remedy for sin. The substitution is exact and it inverts the proverb: Proverbs warns against treating transgression lightly, and Jacob against treating the atonement lightly, so the sentence borrows the KJV's contempt for moral levity and redirects it at unbelief. Proverbs 14:9's second clause, 'but among the righteous there is favour', is also the reward Jacob 6:3 promised the diligent labourers, though nothing verbal survives of it.

links.note: 'And make a mock of the great plan of redemption, which hath been laid for you?' The KJV has one mocker of this construction and he is a fool, and what he mocks is sin. Jacob's mocker mocks the remedy — the substitution is exact and inverted, and it converts a proverb about moral levity into a charge of blasphemy. Held at moderate: three words, and 'make a mock of' had independent currency in nineteenth-century English, so the phrase could arrive without Proverbs. What argues for the source is the KJV's own restriction of the idiom to a single verse about sin.
links.whyNot: Three words, and Jacob's preposition is 'of' where Proverbs has 'at'. The idiom was live in ordinary English and needs no biblical source.

pericopes.text: Know ye not that if ye will do these things, that the power of the redemption and the resurrection which is in Christ, will bring you to stand with shame and awful guilt before the bar of God,

links.text: And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.

provenance.other: 'Shame and everlasting contempt' occurs in exactly one KJV verse. A sweep of text/kjv.json for verses holding both a rising of the dead and shame returns three candidates, of which only Daniel 12:2 makes the resurrection issue in shame; Psalm 109:28 and 1 Corinthians 15:34 are unrelated.
provenance.significance: Daniel 12:2 is the Old Testament's one two-outcome resurrection: some awake to everlasting life and some to shame. Jacob 6:9-11 has both halves and keeps Daniel's order — 'the resurrection which is in Christ, will bring you to stand with shame and awful guilt before the bar of God' at 6:9, and 'until ye shall obtain eternal life' at 6:11. The pair is what carries the link; either half alone would be nothing. Daniel supplies the structure and the New Testament supplies the courtroom, since the resurrection is 'in Christ', which is Paul's phrase and not Daniel's.

links.note: Proposed on the argument rather than the wording, in the manner CONVENTIONS §0a licenses. Nothing is reproduced: Jacob has 'shame' where Daniel has 'shame and everlasting contempt', and 'eternal life' where Daniel has 'everlasting life'. What is worth recording is that the KJV joins resurrection to shame exactly once, and that Jacob's two outcomes are Daniel's two outcomes in Daniel's sequence. Note also that 'the bar of God' occurs in no KJV verse; the KJV's forensic image is the judgment seat (Romans 14:10, 2 Corinthians 5:10), and the bar is the Book of Mormon's own furniture, carried through to 6:13.
links.whyNot: Two words in common across three verses of Jacob, and 'shame' is the obvious English for the affect being described. A writer imagining a last judgment would reach for shame without Daniel's help, and the resurrection-to-life half of the pair is a New Testament commonplace.

pericopes.text: and according to the power of justice? for justice cannot be denied. That ye must go away into that lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames are unquenchable, and whose smoke ascendeth up forever and ever? which lake of fire and brimstone, is endless torment.

links.text: And the devil that deceived them was cast into the lake of fire and brimstone, where the beast and the false prophet are, and shall be tormented day and night for ever and ever.

provenance.route: Revelation 20:10 + Revelation 14:11 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: The exact phrase 'lake of fire and brimstone' occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is Revelation 20:10 — not 19:20, which reads 'a lake of fire burning with brimstone', and not 21:8, which reads 'the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone'. 'Ascendeth up for ever and ever' likewise occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Revelation 14:11, of the smoke of the tormented. 'Unquenchable' occurs in two, Matthew 3:12 and Luke 3:17, both of the chaff.
provenance.significance: Two KJV singletons from two different chapters of Revelation, fused into one sentence, and the fusion supplies what neither verse has alone. Revelation 20:10 has the lake but the smoke is not mentioned; Revelation 14:11 has the smoke ascending for ever but no lake. Jacob 6:10 has 'that lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames are unquenchable, and whose smoke ascendeth up forever and ever'. Recover the contexts and the borrowing is pointed: Revelation 20:10 is where the devil goes, with the beast and the false prophet, and Revelation 14:11 is the torment of those who worshipped the beast. Jacob 6:8 has just listed his hearers' offences as a refusal to hear the prophets and a mockery of redemption — the mirror image of false prophecy and false worship — and 6:10 sends them where Revelation sends the originals. The addition 'which lake of fire and brimstone, is endless torment' then glosses the borrowed image with a term the KJV does not use: 'endless torment' occurs in no KJV verse.

links.note: 'That ye must go away into that lake of fire and brimstone, whose flames are unquenchable, and whose smoke ascendeth up forever and ever?' Five words from one singleton, five from another, plus the Baptist's 'unquenchable'. Catalogued as a quotation on the two exact runs; both are far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and neither is among his.
